title: feat(google-mail): Add threading support (thread_id, In-Reply-To, References, get-email)
cleaned_text: feat(google-mail): Add threading support (thread_id, In-Reply-To, References, get-email) Problem Emails sent via the Gmail MCP tool ( send-email ) cannot be threaded correctly for recipients . The threadId parameter only groups messages on the sender's Gmail — recipients see each reply as a separate conversation. This is because: send-email has no parameters for thread_id , in_reply_to , or references headers There is no get-email action to retrieve the Message-ID header from a sent/received message Without knowing the Gmail-assigned Message-ID , it's impossible to set proper In-Reply-To and References headers on replies Background Per RFC 2822 and Gmail's threading logic, recipient-side threading requires: In-Reply-To: References: Subject: Re: The threadId in the Gmail API request body only affects the sender's mailbox. Recipients rely entirely on these RFC headers. Proposed Changes 1. Add threading parameters to send-email and create-draft thread_id (string, optional) — Gmail thread ID for sender-side threading in_reply_to (string, optional) — RFC 2822 Message-ID of the email being replied to references (string[], optional) — List of Message-IDs from the conversation chain 2. Add new get-email action message_id (string, required) — The ID of the message to retrieve format (enum, optional) — full , metadata , minimal , raw metadata_headers (string[], optional) — Specific headers to return (e.g., ["Message-ID", "In-Reply-To", "References"] ) 3. Backend: pass threading headers through to Gmail API The invoke-action backend needs to: Include threadId in the Gmail API send request body Set In-Reply-To and References in the raw MIME when provided Return Message-ID header in get-email responses Intended Workflow Receive/find an email → note its Gmail id Call get-email with format=metadata , metadata_headers=["Message-ID"] → get the RFC Message-ID Call send-email with thread_id , in_reply_to= , references=[ ] , subject="Re: ..." Email threads correctly for both sender AND recipient ✅ Reference Implementation I have a working fork with the client-side changes (parameters, prompts, tools, configuration): https://github.com/frankhli843/agent-toolkit/tree/fix/gmail-threading-support Happy to open a PR if helpful.

cleaned_text: fix: upgrade dependencies and base image to resolve Trivy-reported CVEs Summary A Trivy scan of the Docker image built from main (v2.1.3) found 10 critical and 86 high vulnerabilities, 87 of them fixable. This PR removes every finding Trivy reports as fixable. | Before | After OS (Debian) | 5 critical, 57 high, 113 medium, 106 low · 13 fixable | 0 critical, 44 high, 55 medium, 59 low · 0 fixable Python packages | 5 critical, 29 high, 33 medium, 8 low · 74 fixable | 0 Critical findings that are now fixed: fastmcp (CVE-2026-32871), Authlib (CVE-2026-27962), PyJWT (CVE-2026-102268), anyio (CVE-2026-63374), h11 (CVE-2025-43859). Changes Dependencies ( pyproject.toml , uv.lock ) fastmcp 2.13.0 → 3.4.7. It stays on 3.x because fastmcp 4.x requires mcp>=2 , which conflicts with the current mcp<2.0.0 constraint. python-dotenv 1.1.0 → 1.2.2 Ran uv lock --upgrade to pick up patched transitive dependencies: Authlib, PyJWT, starlette, mcp, anyio, h11, cryptography, urllib3, python-multipart, requests, idna, Pygments. The existing pydantic>=2.11,<2.12 pin is kept. Dockerfile Builder and runtime images move from Debian bookworm to trixie ( uv:python3.10-trixie-slim , python:3.10-slim-trixie ). This removes about 120 OS findings. The runtime stage runs apt-get upgrade to pick up Debian security updates (OpenSSL, tzdata). The runtime stage removes pip , setuptools and wheel from the system Python. The app runs from /app/.venv and never uses them, but they carried 9 CVEs, including vendored jaraco.context and wheel . title: feat: add opt-in GCF response encoding for tool results (RESPONSE_FORMAT=gcf)
cleaned_text: feat: add opt-in GCF response encoding for tool results (RESPONSE_FORMAT=gcf) Summary Adds an opt-in RESPONSE_FORMAT=gcf that encodes tool-result payloads as Graph Compact Format in the content block the model reads, instead of JSON. The repeated field names of a record array (search hits, aggregation buckets, mappings) are factored into a single header, so a response uses fewer tokens when it crosses the LLM boundary. structuredContent is preserved unchanged. Default is json ; nothing changes unless you opt in. Why Benchmarked on Elasticsearch output ( o200k_base ) payload | JSON | GCF | saved search hits (24 uniform docs) | 1144 | 682 | 40.4% terms aggregation (4 buckets) | 96 | 68 | 29.2% index mapping (6 fields) | 134 | 84 | 37.3% total | 1374 | 834 | 39.3% Reproduce: uv run --with tiktoken python benchmarks/gcf_benchmark.py . Lossless Round-trip verified ( decode(encode(x)) == x ) in the benchmark and tests. GCF is verified lossless across 43 billion+ round-trips in 5 formats and 6 languages. Comprehension, not just size The harder question than size is whether a model reads the compact form as accurately as JSON. Generic-profile comprehension is 100% on every frontier model (Claude Opus/Sonnet/Haiku, GPT-5.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro / 3.1 Pro / 3.5 Flash) — 27 runs, 11 models, 4 providers, equal to or better than JSON on every model. https://gcformat.com/guide/benchmarks GCF was reverse-engineered from attention-level research into how BPE tokenization shapes what a transformer represents, and validated by controlled from-scratch training at 1.3B measured causally (not by an LLM judge), so it holds on models that have never seen the format. Four papers (2026, under review): GCF: A Token-Optimized Wire Format for Structured LLM Interactions — https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20579817 Tokenizer-Attention Coupling — https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20925910 Stranded Attention — https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21158886 Developmental Atlas of Attention Head Specialization — https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21205389 Already adopted The same opt-in pattern is already in other MCP servers and tools: Wazuh-MCP-Server (SIEM MCP), the same RESPONSE_FORMAT=gcf option Chrome DevTools MCP (Google), an experimentalGcfFormat flag mcp-cisco-support, 28.5% fewer tokens on Cisco API data netclaw (network-automation MCP) OmniRoute (LLM gateway) Zero new footprint gcf-python is a zero-dependency package, pinned exact. Design (deliberately conservative) Opt-in and additive. One env var, default json , existing behavior unchanged. Middleware, not a serializer swap. on_call_tool re-encodes only the model-facing text block; structuredContent is preserved verbatim, so the tool's output schema still validates and non-model clients keep receiving JSON. Fail-safe. Any encoding error — including a value outside GCF's canonical int64 numeric domain, which GCF rejects rather than silently approximating — leaves the original result untouched. A tool call is never dropped over encoding. Tests uv run pytest tests/unit/ — the middleware suite covers encoding, structuredContent preservation, JSON/non-JSON handling, out-of-domain fallback, and env gating. All existing tests unchanged. Changes File | Change src/response_format.py | new: GcfResponseMiddleware + RESPONSE_FORMAT selection src/server.py | register the middleware when RESPONSE_FORMAT=gcf tests/unit/server/test_gcf_response_middleware.py | new: encoding + fallback + env tests pyproject.toml / uv.lock | add gcf-python (pinned exact ==2.6.0 ) README.md | document the RESPONSE_FORMAT=gcf option benchmarks/gcf_benchmark.py | reproducible JSON vs GCF token benchmark

title: HTTP transport should default to 127.0.0.1, not 0.0.0.0
cleaned_text: HTTP transport should default to 127.0.0.1, not 0.0.0.0 Summary When using the streamable-http or sse transport modes, the server defaults to host: "0.0.0.0" (all interfaces). This was identified during a formal code review conducted by our team as part of a security vetting assessment. Impact In any environment where the server is accessible beyond the developer's workstation (e.g., a shared development server, a misconfigured firewall, or a container with host networking), the MCP endpoint becomes network-reachable without requiring authentication if MCP_API_KEY is not set. Even with an API key set, binding to all interfaces unnecessarily expands the network attack surface for a tool that is intended for local developer use. Evidence helm/elasticsearch-mcp-server/values.yaml sets transport: streamable-http and host: "0.0.0.0" as defaults. src/server.py reads the host value from configuration without enforcing a localhost-only restriction for HTTP transports. Recommended fix For HTTP-based transports intended for local developer use, default host to 127.0.0.1 rather than 0.0.0.0 . Operators who genuinely need network-accessible deployments can override this explicitly. Consider adding a warning or error if host: "0.0.0.0" is combined with an empty or missing MCP_API_KEY . Context This issue was identified during a Verification & Validation review for use in our environment.

title: set_privacy_settings silently replaces all privacy rules and can open phone/last seen/profile photo to everyone
cleaned_text: set_privacy_settings silently replaces all privacy rules and can open phone/last seen/profile photo to everyone set_privacy_settings silently replaces all privacy rules and can open phone/last seen/profile photo to everyone telegram_mcp/tools/profile.py , set_privacy_settings builds the rules list from scratch and passes it to account.setPrivacy , which replaces the account's rules for that key. Two consequences: Before (current behavior) Any call where allow_users is empty or unused appends InputPrivacyValueAllowAll() . Example: account has phone number visibility set to *Nobody* in Telegram, the agent is asked to hide the phone from one spammer: set_privacy_settings(key="phone", disallow_users=["@spammer"]) allow_users is empty → the tool sends AllowAll (+ the one disallow exception). The phone becomes visible to everybody ; nothing in the output hints at it ("Privacy settings for phone updated successfully."). Every pre-existing exception (allow/disallow user lists, contacts-only, close friends, premium, etc.) is dropped, because the old rules are never read back. Users that fail to resolve are silently skipped (logged only), so a typo in one username of five still rewrites the rules. After (proposed behavior, patch attached) The tool reads the current rules with account.getPrivacy and merges: the main choice (everybody / contacts / nobody / close friends / premium) and all existing exceptions are kept; the requested users are added to (or moved between) the per-user allow/disallow lists; exceptions go first and the main choice last, the order the official apps send. Nothing is sent unless every requested user resolves: one unknown username aborts with Error: Could not find a requested user; privacy settings were not changed. Naming your own account is refused, and an unencodable rule type from a newer server schema aborts instead of being dropped. Empty call (no users) is refused with an explanation instead of opening the setting to everyone. Covered by tests/test_privacy_settings.py (was/became cases: disallow-one under *Nobody* and under *Everybody*, existing exceptions kept, user moved between lists, no change on unknown user / self / unsupported rule). All 1243 tests pass. The same fix is already merged in my fork: axisrow/telegram-mcp#13. I'll open a PR referencing this issue.

title: fix(profile): set_privacy_settings merges exceptions instead of opening privacy to everyone
cleaned_text: fix(profile): set_privacy_settings merges exceptions instead of opening privacy to everyone Before set_privacy_settings never read the current rules: it built a fresh list and passed it to account.setPrivacy , which replaces the rules for the key. With allow_users empty it sent InputPrivacyValueAllowAll() , so a request like set_privacy_settings(key="phone", disallow_users=["@spammer"]) turned an account whose phone visibility was *Nobody* into *Everybody*, and dropped every existing exception (user allow/disallow lists, contacts-only, close friends). Unresolvable users were silently skipped, and the tool still answered "Privacy settings for phone updated successfully." After Reads the current rules with account.getPrivacy , keeps the main choice and all existing exceptions, and merges the requested users into the per-user allow/disallow lists (a user named in one list leaves the other; exceptions first, main choice last — the order the official apps send). Sends nothing unless every requested user resolves: Error: Could not find a requested user; privacy settings were not changed. Refuses the account itself as an exception, refuses to drop a rule type this build cannot re-encode (schema drift), and refuses an empty call instead of opening the setting to everyone. The key mapping / helper cleanup also drops the per-call re-imports and the unreachable TypeError compatibility branch. Tests tests/test_privacy_settings.py pins the before/after cases: disallow-one under *Nobody* and under *Everybody* (main choice kept, exception first), existing exceptions kept and a user moved between lists, no change on unknown user, self, unsupported rule, and the empty call. Suite: 1243 passed (one run). Closes #324. Mirrors axisrow/telegram-mcp#13, already merged in my fork. 🤖 Generated with Claude Code

title: TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_CHAT_IDS is bypassed via contact_id/group_id tool parameters, and listing tools reveal unallowed chats
cleaned_text: TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_CHAT_IDS is bypassed via contact_id/group_id tool parameters, and listing tools reveal unallowed chats Summary When TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_CHAT_IDS is set, the per-chat allowlist is enforced by @validate_id only for parameters named chat_id , from_chat_id , to_chat_id and channel ( CHAT_PARAM_NAMES in telegram_mcp/runtime.py ). Tools whose chat parameter has a different name skip the check, and several listing tools never filter their output. Before With TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_CHAT_IDS=101 : get_last_interaction(contact_id=202) returns the last messages of user 202's private chat, while get_messages(chat_id=202) is correctly refused — the same chat is readable through a differently named parameter. invite_to_group(group_id=…) , promote_admin(group_id=…) and demote_admin(group_id=…) act on groups outside the allowlist. get_common_chats , get_contact_chats , get_direct_chat_by_contact and get_folder return the titles and IDs of unallowed chats. create_folder(chat_ids=[202, …]) adds an unallowed chat to a newly created folder. The README states that with an allowlist "all other conversations remain completely invisible to the agent", so this is a silent gap between the documented and actual behavior. After (proposed) CHAT_PARAM_NAMES also includes contact_id (the private chat with that contact) and group_id (the administered group). user_id stays out on purpose: it names a member acted on inside an already-checked chat, so all group/contact tools are covered through their existing @validate_id decorators. get_common_chats , get_contact_chats , get_direct_chat_by_contact and get_folder drop chats outside the allowlist. Under an allowlist, get_folder also drops peers it cannot resolve, because they cannot be checked. create_folder checks each resolved chat and refuses an unallowed one. InputPeerSelf ( "me" / Saved Messages) short-circuits the check: the account's own chat has no peer id to check and is always allowed. The README allowlist section lists the newly covered tools. A pull request implementing this follows. Environment telegram-mcp 2.0.1, telegram_mcp/runtime.py ( CHAT_PARAM_NAMES ) Verified with 12 new test cases in tests/test_chat_allowlist.py (each bypass fails on current main and passes with the fix); full suite 1247 passed

title: fix(messages): only delete messages that belong to the given chat
cleaned_text: fix(messages): only delete messages that belong to the given chat Related to #317 — this hardens the server against the class of cross-chat deletion described there. Whether that incident was caused by this server has not been established; see the discussion in the issue. What this changes delete_message and delete_messages_bulk now verify that every ID they are asked to delete actually belongs to chat_id before calling Telegram. If any ID is a message of another chat, nothing is deleted and the tool reports which IDs are foreign. Channel/supergroup deletes are skipped by the check — Telegram scopes those by channel already. Why the old behavior was hazardous for private chats Private chats and basic groups share one account-wide message counter. For them Telethon sends messages.deleteMessages with bare IDs (and Telethon's default revoke=True ), so a delete meant for chat A with a stale or shifted ID removes the message that currently holds that ID in chat B — for both sides . A single tool call with wrong IDs can wipe outgoing messages across several unrelated private chats — the class of loss described in #317, though the cause of that incident has not been established. Telethon.get_messages(entity, ids=...) returns None for an ID that does not belong to that chat, so the check is one extra read before any delete — no extra API surface, no behavior change for correct calls. Tests tests/test_delete_messages.py runs the real Telethon request path against a fake in-memory account where private chats share the counter: delete_message refuses a message belonging to another chat and issues no DeleteMessagesRequest . delete_message still deletes a message that does belong to the chat. delete_messages_bulk refuses atomically when any ID is foreign. delete_messages_bulk deletes a valid set. Channel deletes skip the ownership lookup — covered for both the single-message and the bulk tool (Telegram scopes channel deletes itself). Scope note This PR removes the only plausible server-side path for cross-chat deletions, but it cannot confirm whether the server caused #317 — the reporter's Codex logs did not show delete calls either. 🤖 Generated with Claude Code

title: follow-up to #292: a failed reconnect is not reused; concurrent callers still reconnect serially
cleaned_text: follow-up to #292: a failed reconnect is not reused; concurrent callers still reconnect serially #292 serializes reconnects, but only a *successful* reconnect result is reused: when _force_reconnect fails, the shared "last verified" mark ( _last_conn_verified ) is never set, so each of the N waiting callers runs its own full disconnect+connect (up to 30 s each, telegram_mcp/runtime.py:986-1004 ) — serially. In production (5 s ping ceiling + 30 s reconnect) the second and third callers get killed by the 55 s tool timeout ( runtime.py:171 ) and surface an opaque "GEN-TIMEOUT" instead of the actual reconnect error. Repro (fake client whose connect() sleeps 1 s and raises TimeoutError; 3 concurrent ensure_connected calls): SCENARIO: 3 concurrent tool calls hit one client while the network is down connect() attempts made: 3 wall time for the batch: 7.0s (calls serialize: 1s ping + 2s connect, x3) EXPECTED: 1 reconnect attempt (~2s), all 3 callers reuse its failure (commit 2980601 / #292: "the other callers reuse its result") Suggested fix: cache the outcome (timestamp + error) of the last reconnect under the lock key and replay it to waiters while it is fresh. Happy to open a PR.

title: fix(runtime): replay failed reconnect result to queued callers
cleaned_text: fix(runtime): replay failed reconnect result to queued callers Summary Follow-up to #292 (issue #298): reconnects are serialized per client, but only a *successful* reconnect result was reused. When _force_reconnect failed, every queued caller ran its own full disconnect+connect and hit the 55 s tool timeout with an opaque GEN-TIMEOUT instead of the real reconnect error. Cache the reconnect outcome per client under the same lock key and replay it to waiters while it is fresh ( _RECONNECT_FAILURE_TTL = 30 s ); a successful reconnect clears the cache so the next verification cycle runs normally. Before The connection drops while 3 tool calls share one client (streamable HTTP). Only the first caller actually reconnects; each queued caller ran its own full disconnect+connect (up to 30 s each, serially): SCENARIO: 3 concurrent tool calls hit one client while the network is down connect() attempts made: 3 # one full disconnect+connect per caller wall time for the batch: ~90s # far past the 55s tool timeout -> the 2nd/3rd callers die with: "Error: ... (code: GEN-TIMEOUT)" The last callers got an opaque timeout instead of the actual reconnect error. After The first failed reconnect is cached under the connection lock and replayed to every queued caller while it is fresh: SCENARIO: 3 concurrent tool calls hit one client while the network is down connect() attempts made: 1 -> all 3 callers get the real error, e.g. "Error: Reconnecting to Telegram timed out after 30s." If the network recovers, a successful reconnect clears the cache and the normal verify-ping cycle resumes; a stale failure (older than 30 s) triggers a fresh reconnect attempt. Changes telegram_mcp/runtime.py : _reconnect_once wraps both _force_reconnect call sites in ensure_connected and records (timestamp, error) on failure / clears on success; _raise_cached_reconnect_failure replays a fresh failure on the not is_connected() path instead of repeating the attempt. tests/test_runtime.py : autouse fixture resets the reconnect state dicts (they are keyed by id(client) , which CPython reuses across tests); new tests: 3 concurrent callers with a failing connect() produce exactly one connect/disconnect attempt and all get the original ConnectionError ; a stale cached failure is retried and cleared on success. Tests uv run pytest -q — 1194 passed (full suite, includes the 2 new tests). Fixes #298 🤖 Generated with Claude Code

title: Fix: defer slow google-cloud-bigquery import/client construction past MCP stdio handshake
cleaned_text: Fix: defer slow google-cloud-bigquery import/client construction past MCP stdio handshake Problem main() currently imports google.cloud.bigquery at module load time and constructs BigQueryDatabase (which builds a bigquery.Client ) synchronously, before mcp.server.stdio.stdio_server() opens. That means the process can't read/respond to the MCP initialize handshake until both finish. Measured in isolation: from google.cloud import bigquery # ~35-40s cold (grpcio/protobuf/proto-plus/google-api-core chain) bigquery.Client(credentials=None, ...) # ~5s Several MCP clients (e.g. Claude Code) enforce a connect timeout well under that (30s), so this server reliably loses the race on cold starts, surfacing as a generic "connection timed out" error with no indication of the actual cause. The same anti-pattern shows up again inside handle_call_tool : list_tables / describe_table / execute_query run as plain synchronous calls directly on the asyncio event loop. Any slow query, proxy hop, or credential refresh blocks the *entire process* from servicing stdio for its duration — indistinguishable from a dead server to the client. Fix Move the google.cloud.bigquery / google.oauth2.service_account imports inside BigQueryDatabase. init (added from future import annotations so the service_account.Credentials | None annotation still resolves without eager import). Defer BigQueryDatabase construction to first tool call via an async get_db() helper, using asyncio.to_thread(...) + asyncio.Lock() so it only runs once, off the event loop. Wrap the list_tables / describe_table / execute_query calls in asyncio.to_thread(...) inside handle_call_tool so slow queries/token refreshes no longer block the stdio loop mid-session. Net effect: the stdio handshake completes immediately regardless of import/client-construction cost. That cost doesn't disappear — it moves to the first actual tool call — but it now runs off the event loop, so it trades a hard connect-timeout failure for a slower-but-successful first call, and stops mid-session tool calls from freezing the whole server. Verification python -m py_compile passes. Isolated import of the patched module: ~2.6s, with bigquery confirmed absent from module globals until first BigQueryDatabase construction. Live-tested against two separate BigQuery MCP server entries in Claude Code that were both reliably failing with connection timed out after 30000ms on /mcp reconnect before this change, and now reconnect successfully every time. title: Optional, disclosed sponsored field for search results (opt-in, MIT) — interested?
cleaned_text: Optional, disclosed sponsored field for search results (opt-in, MIT) — interested? Hi — I'm Tal, building Lulu Ads (getlulu.dev), an open-source SDK that lets MCP servers add one optional, disclosed sponsored field to a tool response — model decides if it's relevant, fails open on any error, never touches error responses. Search results are the cleanest fit for this — one labeled item, never touching the real ones. No pricing tiers required — it's CPA-only, 70% of revenue is yours, and it's a single flag you control entirely (on for everyone, off for everyone, or wired to whatever you build later). Free to add, MIT-licensed. Self-serve publisher signup: https://getlulu.dev/publishers Would a PR adding this as an opt-in flag be welcome?

cleaned_text: feat: add opt-in --cache-ttl for repeated Figma reads Description Closes #430. Summary Adds one opt-in server setting, --cache-ttl / CACHE_TTL , that reuses successful Figma reads for a short time. Off by default, in-memory only, max 60m. A hit is labeled with its age. get_figma_data caches the simplified output. download_figma_images caches fill and render URLs only; image bytes are still downloaded and written on every call. Errors are never stored. The cache is owned by startServer so HTTP mode (a new MCP server per request) can hit it. Keys include a hash of the credential, never the raw token. npx figma-developer-mcp --figma-api-key=... --cache-ttl 5m or CACHE_TTL=5m A hit prepends a separate content block, so json and yaml output stays parseable: Note: cached Figma response from 42s ago (TTL 5m). The file may have changed since this was fetched. Test plan [x] pnpm type-check , pnpm lint , prettier --check src , pnpm test (265 passed, 1 skipped) [x] HTTP mode against the real Figma API ( --cache-ttl 20s ): a repeat inside the TTL made no upstream request; after the TTL it fetched again. Image files were rewritten on every download, including cache hits. [ ] stdio transport, image fills against the real API, and 429 responses were not exercised manually

title: Optional short-TTL cache for repeated Figma reads
cleaned_text: Optional short-TTL cache for repeated Figma reads Description: Right now both tools go straight to the Figma REST API on every call. get_figma_data reads /files/{fileKey} and /files/{fileKey}/nodes , and download_figma_images reads /files/{fileKey}/images and /images/{fileKey} . So if an agent asks for the same frame a few times in one session, which happens a lot, each request costs a Tier 1 call. That's what's behind the 429s in #258. To be clear, Framelink itself isn't rate-limiting anything. Figma is, and how much headroom you get depends on the file owner's plan. This matters more now because this server is the fallback when Figma's official remote MCP isn't an option. That one is allowlisted and metered (HN thread). This one just talks REST, so any client can run it. I saw #256, which caches the whole file with no TTL. I'm worried about two side effects. Asking for a single frame ends up pulling the entire document, and a later session can serve a design that no longer matches the file in Figma. What I'm proposing A single, opt-in staleness setting: --cache-ttl / CACHE_TTL (e.g. 5m ), off by default . One value covers both tools, because a node tree and a render of that same node should go stale together. It would only apply to those four reads: File and node responses: cache the raw responses, keyed on a hash of the credential plus fileKey , nodeId , and depth . Image-fill and render URLs: cache these the same way, with format and scale added to the key. Figma expires those URLs anyway, and a short TTL stays well inside that window. The actual image bytes would still be downloaded and written to localPath on every call. Expiry: entries expire at the TTL. Errors are never cached. Visibility: include the cache age in the tool result so the caller knows how fresh the data is. Scope: a server-level flag only, not a tool parameter. It also wouldn't live inside the shared request() helper. What this doesn't do It only dedupes a caller's own repeat requests within the TTL window. It won't raise anyone's plan limits, and it isn't meant as a comment on the official MCP. Happy to put up a PR if this direction sounds reasonable.

title: fix: emit valid CSS for text shadows
cleaned_text: fix: emit valid CSS for text shadows A Figma TEXT node with a drop shadow currently emits 2px 3px 4px 0px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5) as textShadow . Browsers reject the fourth length and compute text-shadow: none , so even an ordinary text drop shadow disappears when the returned CSS is used. Text shadows now use the supported three-length form, 2px 3px 4px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5) . Inner-shadow entries are omitted for TEXT nodes because inset invalidates the entire list, including otherwise valid drop shadows. Non-TEXT box shadows retain their spread and inset values; blur output is unchanged. CSS text-shadow cannot represent Figma spread or inner shadows; this fix does not attempt to emulate either. The grammar is defined in CSS Text Decoration §4. Validation: Same regression tests on base c083d65c7e002923e7cb98f4e3bdafb105e90f6d : 5 failures before, all 9 effects tests pass after. Covers absent/zero/nonzero spread, mixed and inner-only shadows, hidden effects, multiple shadows, blur preservation, and box-shadow compatibility. pnpm test : 256 passed, 1 skipped. The skipped test is the repository's opt-in live Figma integration test; no Figma account or design file was used. pnpm type-check , pnpm lint , pnpm build , pnpm exec prettier --check "src/ /*.ts" , and node scripts/scan-hidden-chars.mjs pass (Node 26.0.0, pnpm 10.10.0). Chrome 147: CSS.supports("text-shadow", before) is false and the computed value is none ; the actual transformed output after this fix is supported and renders a shadow. The non-TEXT computed box shadow is identical before and after. Only the effects transformer and its tests change. No dependencies or generated files change.

title: feat: extract and surface Dev Mode annotations
cleaned_text: feat: extract and surface Dev Mode annotations Motivation ROADMAP.md already listed this as an open item: "Investigate feasibility of pulling in annotations via the Figma API." This PR implements it. Background @figma/rest-api-spec (v0.37.0) publishes AnnotationsTrait as an empty object — the annotations field on nodes isn't typed at all in the generated spec. However, the live Figma REST API does return it on nodes that carry a Dev Mode annotation. I verified this against a real Figma file with an existing annotation — the raw GET /v1/files/:key/nodes response actually contains "annotations": [{ "label": "..." }] on the relevant node — so this isn't based on documentation alone, it's confirmed against live API responses. What changed src/transformers/annotation.ts (new): models the real wire shape ( label , labelMarkdown , properties[].type , categoryId ) since the spec package doesn't, and simplifies it to { label?, properties?: string[], categoryId? } — preferring labelMarkdown over label when both are present, and dropping the property wrapper objects for token efficiency. src/extractors/built-in.ts : new annotationExtractor , added to allExtractors so it's included by default in get_figma_data output. src/extractors/types.ts : added annotations?: SimplifiedAnnotation[] to SimplifiedNode . src/utils/serialize-tree.ts : added annotations= rendering to the default tree output format. title: fix: pass unknown paint types through marked instead of throwing
cleaned_text: fix: pass unknown paint types through marked instead of throwing Problem parsePaint throws on any paint type outside its known set (SOLID, IMAGE, PATTERN, the four gradients), and the throw fails the entire get_figma_data request. Paint types absent from the REST spec do reach real files: on 2026-08-22 we hit Figma code-component CUSTOM paints ( customEffectId: "CodeComponentId:..." plus componentPropAssignments ) on several nodes of a production file, and each one made its whole subtree uncapturable with Error fetching file: Unknown paint type: CUSTOM . Any future paint type Figma ships has the same effect until the transformer learns it. Change Unknown paint types degrade instead of throwing: parsePaint returns { type, unknownPaint: true, raw } , where raw is the untouched Figma paint object, and logs an error line. The fill is marked rather than silently dropped, so consumers can detect it (and still read the raw paint), while the rest of the simplification is unaffected. Adds SimplifiedUnknownFill to the SimplifiedFill union. Backward compatibility Output for all recognized paint types is unchanged. Requests that previously failed outright now succeed with a marked fill entry; nothing that previously succeeded changes shape. Downstream code that switches on fill type (e.g. image download collection matching "IMAGE" ) skips the unknown entry naturally. Validation 4 new vitest cases ( src/tests/unknown-paint.test.ts ): marked passthrough, raw-field preservation, known paints untouched, and stroke parsing surviving a mixed known/unknown paint list. Against the current code, 3 of 4 fail with the exact production error ( Unknown paint type: CUSTOM ); with the change, the full suite passes (254 passed / 1 skipped). tsc --noEmit clean. title: fix: preserve node rotation, true size, ink bounds, and explicit line breaks
cleaned_text:
fix: preserve node rotation, true size, ink bounds, and explicit line breaks Problem The simplifier currently loses three classes of design facts: Rotation. absoluteBoundingBox is the axis-aligned box *around* a rotated node — inflated and corner-anchored. A 100x148.75 rectangle at -18.3° is reported as an unrotated 141.6x172.6 box at the wrong position, and the angle is unrecoverable from the output. Any design with tilted elements (photo collages, decorative scatter, badges) cannot be implemented faithfully from the simplified data: consumers render everything upright and oversized. Ink bounds. For text-on-path and vector nodes, the layout box says nothing about where the rendered ink sits, so an exported asset placed at the reported box lands in the wrong place. Explicit line breaks. Figma's (what Shift+Return inserts) passes through unescaped while 
 / are escaped to 
 markers, so a designer's manual break silently collapses into a space in HTML and the text re-wraps differently from the design. Root cause for 1–2: the REST requests never pass geometry=paths , so Figma never sends relativeTransform / size , and the transformer only reads bounding boxes. Change Request geometry=paths on getRawFile / getRawNode . When a node (or its parent group) is rotated beyond a 0.05° epsilon, emit rotation (degrees, Figma sign: counter-clockwise positive; CSS equivalent is rotate(- deg) with transform-origin: top left ), and switch dimensions / locationRelativeToParent to the true unrotated size and the pre-rotation top-left from relativeTransform (already parent-relative). Children of rotated groups take this path even when locally unrotated so nested transforms compose. Emit renderBounds (parent-relative absoluteRenderBounds ) for vector-class nodes ( TEXT_PATH , VECTOR , BOOLEAN_OPERATION , STAR , LINE , POLYGON ) when ink differs from the layout box by more than 1px. Treat like 
 / in both the line splitter and the markdown escaper. Backward compatibility Unrotated nodes under unrotated parents produce byte-identical output (covered by a test). New fields are optional additions to SimplifiedLayout . geometry=paths increases the raw REST payload server-side; the simplified output only grows by the new fields on affected nodes. Validation 5 new vitest cases ( src/tests/rotation-transform.test.ts ); full suite passes (255 tests). Validated against a production Figma file: 30 rotated nodes (a marketing collage, including nested book+icon groups) cross-checked against independent Figma plugin-API measurements of the same nodes — rotation matched within 0.12°, sizes and positions exactly, and nested groups composed to the correct absolute angles (-30° / 17.73° / 2.77°).

title: fix(common): validate image URLs against allowlist to prevent SSRF
cleaned_text: fix(common): validate image URLs against allowlist to prevent SSRF Summary Adds an allowlist check on image URLs before the server fetches them in downloadFigmaImage ( src/utils/common.ts ). Today the URL is passed straight to fetch() after coming out of a Figma API response ( GetImageFillsResponse.meta.images / GetImagesResponse.images ). If the returned URL is ever crafted — e.g. a compromised Figma account/file, a malicious workspace shared with the caller, or a MITM against api.figma.com — the server-side fetch() would happily hit any host, including 127.0.0.1 , 10.0.0.0/8 , or cloud metadata endpoints like http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ . This is a classic CWE-918 (Server-Side Request Forgery) pattern. The change is small and defence-in-depth: it does not weaken the current happy path. Trusted Figma CDN URLs ( *.figma.com , figma-alpha-api.s3.*.amazonaws.com , *.figmausercontent.com ) still pass, but the server refuses to fetch anything else, refuses non-HTTPS schemes ( http:// , file:// , gopher:// , dict:// , javascript: , data: ), and explicitly blocks loopback / link-local / GCP metadata hosts even if they somehow matched a pattern. Vulnerability details CWE: CWE-918 (Server-Side Request Forgery) File: src/utils/common.ts , downloadFigmaImage() Sink: fetch(imageUrl, { method: "GET" }) on line 39 (pre-fix line 32) Data flow: Figma API JSON response → services/figma.ts → passed as imageUrl argument → fetch() The imageUrl string is trusted implicitly because it comes back from api.figma.com . It is not sanitised, not scheme-restricted, and not host-restricted. The MCP tool download_figma_images will reach this code path whenever a client asks for image downloads. Fix New helper src/utils/url-validation.ts exports assertSafeImageUrl(url) : Parses the URL via WHATWG URL (throws on syntactically invalid input). Requires protocol === "https:" . Rejects localhost , 127.0.0.1 , [::1] , 169.254.* , metadata.google.internal explicitly. Requires the hostname to match one of: *.figma.com , *.amazonaws.com , *.figmausercontent.com . Called once, immediately before fetch() in downloadFigmaImage . Test results Two new test files, 31 assertions in total, all passing under the existing pnpm test suite (16 files, 203 passed, 1 skipped — same skipped integration test as before): src/tests/url-validation.test.ts — 6 tests covering the primary allow/deny matrix. src/tests/url-validation-bypass.test.ts — 25 adversarial cases from the SSRF checklist: Decimal / hex / octal encodings of 127.0.0.1 ( 2130706433 , 0x7f000001 , 017700000001 ) Short-form loopback ( 127.1 , 127.0.1 ) IPv6 loopback variants ( [::1] , [0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1] ) RFC1918 ranges ( 10.0.0.1 , 192.168.1.1 , 172.16.0.1 ) Cloud metadata endpoints (AWS 169.254.169.254 , Alibaba 100.100.100.200 , GCP metadata.google.internal ) nip.io -style resolvers Non-HTTPS schemes ( gopher:// , dict:// , ftp:// , javascript: , data: ) Userinfo tricks ( https://figma.com@evil.com/ , https://evil.com#@figma.com/ ) Look-alike hostnames ( figma.com.evil.com , evilfigma.com , figmausercontent.com.evil.tld ) Legitimate Figma URLs ( s3-alpha-sig.figma.com , figma-alpha-api.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com , cdn.figmausercontent.com ) are asserted to still pass, so the fix is non-breaking for the intended flow. Full test run: Test Files 16 passed | 1 skipped (17) Tests 203 passed | 1 skipped (204) pnpm type-check , pnpm lint , and the lefthook pre-commit chain (scan-hidden-chars / format / lint / type-check) also pass. Proof of concept The minimum harness needed to demonstrate the pre-patch behaviour is a direct call to the exported downloadFigmaImage , since that is the exact entry point exercised by the download_figma_images MCP tool via src/utils/image-processing.ts:111 . Save as poc-ssrf.mjs at the repo root and run against main (pre-patch) vs. this branch: // poc-ssrf.mjs import http from "node:http"; import { downloadFigmaImage } from "./dist/utils/common.js"; // after pnpm build // Stand up a local "internal service" the server has no business reaching. const internal = http.createServer((req, res) => { console.log("[internal] hit by SSRF:", req.url); res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "image/png" }); res.end("SECRET_INTERNAL_DATA"); }).listen(18080, "127.0.0.1"); // Simulates a crafted URL that reaches downloadFigmaImage — this is what // would happen if the Figma API response were tampered with (compromised // account, malicious shared file, MITM on api.figma.com). try { const out = await downloadFigmaImage( "leak.png", "/tmp/ssrf-poc", "http://127.0.0.1:18080/etc/passwd", ); console.log("[poc] SSRF succeeded — wrote", out); } catch (e) { console.log("[poc] blocked:", e.message); } finally { internal.close(); } Before this patch: [internal] hit by SSRF: /etc/passwd is logged and /tmp/ssrf-poc/leak.png contains SECRET_INTERNAL_DATA . The same PoC works against http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ on any EC2 host that runs the server. After this patch: [poc] blocked: Refusing to fetch image over insecure protocol: http: . Swapping to https://127.0.0.1:18080/... yields Refusing to fetch image from internal address: 127.0.0.1 ; swapping to https://evil.com/x.png yields Image URL hostname not in allowlist: evil.com. Expected a Figma CDN domain. Security analysis and adversarial review Before submitting we deliberately tried to disprove this finding. Two things could have made it a non-issue: "The URL isn't attacker-controlled." True in the direct sense — a random MCP client can't just pass an arbitrary URL to fetch() ; the URL has to come back inside a Figma API JSON body. But the trust boundary is still wrong. Reaching this sink requires one of (a) a compromised Figma account or malicious shared file whose image references point at attacker-chosen URLs, (b) a MITM on the TLS connection to api.figma.com (rogue CA / corporate proxy), or (c) supply-chain compromise on the Figma side. None of those are hypothetical for a tool that runs inside developer environments and CI. Treating any fetch() of an externally-influenced URL as needing an allowlist is standard SSRF hygiene. "The server is only bound to 127.0.0.1 so nobody can reach it anyway." This finding is about outbound requests the server itself makes, not inbound reachability. The default HTTP bind ( 127.0.0.1 ) and stdio mode don't change the SSRF surface — the server still initiates the internal fetch on behalf of whatever caller is on the box. Given that, the fix is scoped intentionally: it does not try to be a general egress filter, only a guard on this one image-download path where the URL comes from a third-party API. Known limitations we considered: The patch does not set redirect: "error" on the underlying fetch() . Undici's default is redirect: "follow" , so a compromised Figma-hosted URL that returns a 302 to an internal target would still bypass validation at redirect time. That is a follow-up worth doing but felt out-of-scope for this PR — happy to add it here if you'd prefer a single change. ^[\w.-]+\.amazonaws\.com$ allows any AWS-hosted bucket, not just Figma's. Tightening to figma-alpha-api.s3.*.amazonaws.com is possible; we kept the broader pattern to avoid breaking if Figma rotates buckets/regions. Open to narrowing if you have a canonical list. No behavioural change for stdio-mode single-user-local usage; the guard is purely additive. Nothing else in the tree calls fetch() on a URL that originates from a Figma API response, so a single call-site is sufficient. assertSafeImageUrl is a pure function with no side effects, making it easy to reason about and to extend later.

title: Security: Critical Remote Code Execution (RCE) via Sandbox Escape
cleaned_text: Security: Critical Remote Code Execution (RCE) via Sandbox Escape I have discovered a critical Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability in the AWSResourceQuerier.execute_query method. The current security implementation relies on an AST-based import check and a restricted builtins dictionary, both of which are easily bypassed. Vulnerabilities: AST-Import Bypass: The CodeExecutor only checks for 'import' and 'from ... import' statements. It does not block the use of the built-in import () function. Permissive Builtins: The builtins dictionary explicitly allows ' import ' and 'getattr' (lines 122-123), providing a direct path to import any module, including 'os' or 'subprocess'. Exploit Example: An attacker can provide the following code snippet: os = import ('os') result = os.popen('whoami').read() This payload bypasses the AST check and uses the allowed import function to gain full shell access to the host server. Impact: Full compromise of the MCP server and potential theft of AWS credentials stored in environment variables. Recommendation: Remove the use of exec() on user-provided code. If dynamic execution is required, use a strictly isolated environment such as a separate Docker container with no network access or a specialized safe-eval library. Do not include ' import ' or 'getattr' in the allowed builtins.

title: feat: add MYSQL_POOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT to close idle pool connections
cleaned_text: feat: add MYSQL_POOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT to close idle pool connections The mysql2 pool never closes idle connections by default, so each running server keeps its connections open until the MySQL server's wait_timeout , even when it runs no queries. With many idle MCP clients pointed at one server, this can exhaust max_connections . MYSQL_POOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT (milliseconds) makes the pool close connections that stay idle longer than that. Invalid values are logged and ignored; when the variable is unset, behaviour is unchanged. Note: while the timeout is set, mysql2's eviction timer keeps the event loop alive, so a stdio server whose client went away without a signal no longer exits when MySQL drops its last socket. The server does not exit on stdin close today either; that is left for a separate change. 🤖 Generated with Claude Code

title: fix(server): keep serving when the DB is unreachable at startup instead of exiting
cleaned_text: fix(server): keep serving when the DB is unreachable at startup instead of exiting fix(server): keep serving when the DB is unreachable at startup instead of exiting Fixes #150. Also reported in #74. Problem When the configured MySQL server is unreachable at launch (intranet host, VPN/tunnel down, DNS failure, DB still booting), the server exits immediately after answering the MCP initialize handshake — silently. Reproduction: git clone https://github.com/benborla/mcp-server-mysql && cd mcp-server-mysql npm install && npm run build MYSQL_HOST=nonexistent.invalid MYSQL_PORT=33061 MYSQL_USER=u MYSQL_PASS=p MYSQL_DB=freight \ node dist/index.js Over stdio, send newline-delimited JSON-RPC: initialize → notifications/initialized → tools/list → tools/call ( mysql_query , SELECT 1 ). Result on current main : initialize ✅ and tools/list ✅ are answered, then the process calls exit 1 ~180 ms in. stderr is completely empty — the failure is invisible. The tools/call request never gets a response (the process is already dead). MCP clients interpret this as a crash and reconnect-loop the server; most circuit-break it after a few attempts, so the server never becomes usable. Root cause Two mechanisms kill the process on DB unavailability: Eager startup connectivity check ( index.ts , in the server factory): the server does pool.getConnection() once at startup and calls safeExit(1) (→ process.exit(1) ) on *any* failure. A startup connectivity check is treated as fatal. Global error handlers : process.on("uncaughtException") and process.on("unhandledRejection") also call safeExit(1) , so a connection error surfacing outside a request handler kills the server. Both are silent in the default configuration because log() in src/utils/index.ts is a no-op unless ENABLE_LOGGING=true — so the log("error", ...) right before safeExit(1) produces no output. Behavior change | Before | After DB unreachable at startup | process.exit(1) ~180 ms after initialize / tools/list , silent (no stderr without ENABLE_LOGGING ) | Warning on stderr, server keeps serving tools/call while DB down | No response (process dead) | Normal tool error result, e.g. Error: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND nonexistent.invalid DB comes back later | Client must restart the server (or it circuit-broke already) | Next query succeeds, no restart needed uncaughtException / unhandledRejection | process.exit(1) | Logged (stderr) and process continues Pool-level error event | Unhandled EventEmitter error → crash via uncaughtException | Logged (stderr), pool continues Fix Three minimal changes: index.ts — startup check : on connection failure, write a warning to stderr (always visible, unlike log() ) and continue serving. Queries return normal tool errors until the database is reachable. index.ts — uncaughtException / unhandledRejection handlers : log-and-continue instead of safeExit(1) . Errors are written to stderr so they remain visible with ENABLE_LOGGING off. src/db/index.ts — getPool() : defensive, log-only 'error' handlers on both the promise pool and the underlying core pool, so a pool-level error event never surfaces as an unhandled EventEmitter error. safeExit is intentionally kept for SIGINT/SIGTERM shutdown errors and for genuine server startup failures (transport binding, etc.) — only DB-availability-driven exits are removed. Test evidence Verified on macOS 15.6 arm64, node v24.5.0, with a stdio harness that spawns the built server, performs initialize → notifications/initialized → tools/list → tools/call ( SELECT 1 ), then holds the connection for 20 s. MYSQL_HOST=nonexistent.invalid MYSQL_PORT=33061 MYSQL_USER=u MYSQL_PASS=p MYSQL_DB=freight : | unpatched main (b9c714e) | this branch initialize / tools/list | ok / ok | ok / ok tools/call | no response — process already dead | isError: true , content Error: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND nonexistent.invalid stderr | *(empty)* | MySQL server unreachable at startup: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND nonexistent.invalid — continuing to serve; queries will return errors until the database is reachable exit | code=1 at=180ms | alive after 20 s (exit 0 is the harness's final SIGTERM handled gracefully) With a reachable database, behavior is unchanged: SELECT 1 returns normally. npm run lint:eslint and npm run build pass. npx vitest run tests/unit : 147 passed, 4 failed — the 4 failures ( tests/unit/query.test.ts , transaction-permission assertions) are pre-existing on main (identical result before this patch). Note: npm run test:unit fails on main regardless of this change because vitest.unit.config.ts is referenced by package.json but not committed to the repository.

title: No query timeout: a slow SELECT never returns and the MCP client hangs forever
cleaned_text: No query timeout: a slow SELECT never returns and the MCP client hangs forever Summary There is no query timeout. MYSQL_CONNECT_TIMEOUT (added in v2.0.7) covers establishing the connection, and MYSQL_QUEUE_LIMIT covers the pool queue — but once a query is running, nothing bounds it. If a SELECT takes longer than the caller is willing to wait, mysql_query simply never returns. For an interactive MCP client that is merely slow. For an autonomous agent it is worse than an error: the tool call has no result, no partial output and no failure, so the agent sits on it indefinitely. In our case a sub-agent stayed "still running", reporting the same progress, until a human noticed and killed it. An error after N seconds would have been recoverable; silence is not. Environment @benborla29/mcp-server-mysql 2.0.9 (latest on npm at the time of writing, published 2026-06-19) launched via npx , stdio transport read-only config: ALLOW_INSERT_OPERATION / ALLOW_UPDATE_OPERATION / ALLOW_DELETE_OPERATION all false What I checked before filing Grepping the published dist/ for timeout-related identifiers returns only: MYSQL_CONNECT_TIMEOUT connectTimeout So the gap looks structural rather than a misconfiguration on my side. The pool is created with waitForConnections: true , which means a hung query can also block *subsequent* callers until queueLimit is reached — one stuck query degrades the whole server, not just its own call. Suggested fix Something like MYSQL_QUERY_TIMEOUT (ms, 0 /unset = current behaviour), applied per query. Two implementations that would both work: Server-side ceiling for SELECT — inject the optimizer hint SELECT /*+ MAX_EXECUTION_TIME(ms) */ … . MySQL enforces it itself (5.7.8+), so the query is actually stopped rather than abandoned. Only applies to SELECT , which for a read-only server is the common case. Client-side race + KILL QUERY — bound the promise and issue KILL QUERY on expiry, so the connection is returned to the pool instead of leaking. Either way the important part is that the tool call returns an error instead of hanging: an MCP client can retry, narrow the query, or tell the user. It cannot do anything with silence. Workaround for anyone hitting this now Write the hint into the query yourself: SELECT /*+ MAX_EXECUTION_TIME(30000) */ ... It is an optimizer hint, i.e. a comment, so a server that does not support it ignores it rather than failing. We enforce it with a client-side pre-tool hook that rejects any SELECT reaching the server without one — but that is a workaround around the server, and it only protects clients that happen to have such a hook. Happy to test a patch against a production-sized dataset if that helps.

title: Server exits immediately after initialize handshake — never responds to tools/list (all versions)
cleaned_text: Server exits immediately after initialize handshake — never responds to tools/list (all versions) Summary The stdio server answers the MCP initialize request and then terminates roughly 0.4 s later, without ever replying to tools/list . Every MCP client therefore fails during connection setup. This is not an npx startup-timeout problem: running the entry point directly with node fails identically, on every published version. Versions tested Version | Exit code | tools/list 1.0.21 | 1 | no response 2.0.5 | 0 | no response 2.0.7 | 0 | no response 2.0.8 | 1 | no response 2.0.9 (latest) | 1 | no response Environment Node.js v22.23.1 Linux 6.18.48-1-lts (x86_64) Database: MariaDB 12.3.3 , TCP 127.0.0.1:3306 , user root , single database mode Client: Pi's native MCP ( pi mcp list reports connection closed during setup ) Reproduction No MCP client required: export MYSQL_DATABASE= MYSQL_HOST=localhost MYSQL_USER=root \ MYSQL_PASSWORD= MYSQL_PORT=3306 printf '%s\n' \ '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"repro","version":"1.0"}}}' \ | npx -y --package=@benborla29/mcp-server-mysql -- mcp-server-mysql echo "exit=$?" Observed: a valid initialize result is written to stdout, then the process exits with code 1 immediately, and stderr is completely empty . Keeping stdin open and then sending notifications/initialized followed by tools/list produces no reply at all, and the next write fails with a broken pipe: [initialize] replied, id=1, capabilities: [resources, tools] [0.4s] >>> process exited, code 1 (stderr: empty) [tools/list] >>> BrokenPipeError What is *not* the cause Each of these was tested and ruled out: Protocol version. The server negotiates 2024-11-05 , 2025-03-26 and 2025-06-18 and returns a valid result for each one. Credentials or connectivity. With the same environment the handshake succeeds, and the same host/port/user/password work with the mysql client against the same database. npx . Invoking the entry point directly, node node_modules/@benborla29/mcp-server-mysql/dist/index.js , shows the identical initialize-then-exit behaviour. Cold cache. A warm npx start takes about 1 s, well inside any client timeout. The test harness. Two unrelated MCP servers ( engram , context7 ) were driven through the exact same JSON-RPC sequence by the same script, stayed alive and returned their tool lists normally. Note that this contradicts the root-cause analysis in #108, which reports that calling the server directly with node works. In this environment direct node invocation fails the same way npx does. Additional observations The initialize result advertises capabilities.resources as an empty object {} . Resources are therefore declared but never served, which makes conforming clients issue a resources/list request that also goes unanswered. serverInfo.version is surfaced as the literal string vundefined in the tool description: [MySQL MCP Server [vundefined]] Run SQL queries... . Expected behaviour The process should stay alive after answering initialize , reply to tools/list , and only exit when stdin is closed. Version 2.0.9 (latest at the time of writing)

title: Stale reads under REPEATABLE READ: pooled connection can keep a frozen read view (open transaction) across calls
cleaned_text: Stale reads under REPEATABLE READ: pooled connection can keep a frozen read view (open transaction) across calls Describe the bug With MySQL running at its default REPEATABLE READ isolation level, mysql_query can persistently return stale data : rows committed by other sessions are not visible through the MCP server, while a fresh mysql CLI connection against the same database sees them immediately. The stale view can survive for the entire lifetime of the MCP server process; restarting the server (or switching the affected session to READ COMMITTED ) makes the latest values visible again. This is server-side behavior (independent of the MCP client). The root cause appears to be how pooled connections are managed in src/db/index.ts . Analysis (based on the v2.0.9 source) The server keeps a long-lived mysql2 pool ( connectionLimit: 10 , enableKeepAlive: true ). mysql2 's Pool.release() returns the raw connection to the pool without resetting any MySQL session state — an open transaction or a non-default session variable on a connection carries over to the next caller of that connection. The read path ( executeReadOnlyQuery ) wraps every single-statement SELECT in an explicit transaction and toggles per-connection session state on every call: SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY START TRANSACTION -- what mysql2's beginTransaction() sends SELECT ... ROLLBACK SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ WRITE Under InnoDB REPEATABLE READ , a transaction's consistent read view is established at its first read and remains frozen for the lifetime of the transaction (see the MySQL 8.0 docs, "Consistent Nonlocking Reads"). Any path that returns a pooled connection without a matching COMMIT / ROLLBACK therefore leaves that connection inside an open transaction with a frozen snapshot . From that point on, any statement executed on that connection keeps reading the snapshot taken when the transaction began — the server appears to "never see the latest values". Three code paths can leave (or perpetuate) a pooled connection inside such a stale open transaction: Swallowed rollback failure on the error path. In executeReadOnlyQuery , if connection.rollback() itself throws (query error, dropped connection, network interruption), the failure is caught and explicitly ignored ( "Ignore errors during cleanup" ), and the connection is still released in the finally block — with the transaction still open. Client abort / timeout with no statement timeout. There is no query timeout on the server side (see #148), so when an MCP client times out or aborts a tool call, the in-flight START TRANSACTION plus slow query can outlive the request. A hung query holds its connection — and its open transaction — indefinitely. executeQuery (the plain helper used by the mysql://tables/* schema resources) has no transaction management at all. On a connection that carries a lingering open transaction, it executes *inside* that transaction, returns frozen-snapshot data, and never ends the transaction — so the stale state persists across many subsequent calls. (A statement issued while a transaction is already active executes within it; only COMMIT / ROLLBACK ends it.) Once one pooled connection is poisoned this way, every tool call routed to it returns stale data until the process is restarted — which matches the observed "always stale under REPEATABLE READ" behavior. The symptom is specific to REPEATABLE READ : under READ COMMITTED a fresh snapshot is taken for each statement, so a poisoned connection does not exhibit it. Steps to reproduce MySQL 8.x with the default isolation level: SELECT @@transaction_isolation; → REPEATABLE-READ . Seed data: CREATE TABLE t (id INT PRIMARY KEY, v INT); INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 1); Start the MCP server (default configuration) and call mysql_query with SELECT v FROM t WHERE id = 1 → returns 1 . Poison one pooled connection (any one of): KILL (from SHOW PROCESSLIST ) for the MCP server's connection while a mysql_query call is in flight, or drop the connection via a network interruption, so the server-side ROLLBACK cannot run; or abort/timeout the tool call on the MCP client side while the query is in flight (no statement timeout on the server side, see #148). In a separate session: UPDATE t SET v = 2 WHERE id = 1; COMMIT; Call mysql_query again with SELECT v FROM t WHERE id = 1 : the poisoned connection returns 1 (stale), and repeated calls on it keep returning 1 ; meanwhile mysql -e "SELECT v FROM t WHERE id = 1" shows 2 . Restart the MCP server → the query returns 2 . Expected behavior Every mysql_query call should see all data committed at the time the query runs (a fresh read view per call), regardless of the server isolation level and regardless of earlier errors or client aborts on pooled connections. Workarounds Restarting the MCP server clears the poisoned connections. Running MySQL (or the relevant sessions) at READ COMMITTED avoids the symptom, since the read view is established per statement. Suggested fixes (any one of these should resolve it) Don't wrap single-statement reads in an explicit transaction. With autocommit on, each statement is its own transaction and gets a fresh read view under REPEATABLE READ . The per-call SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY / READ WRITE toggle is then unnecessary (it also leaves the session in read-only state if the flow is interrupted between the two statements, which can sporadically break later write calls with "Cannot execute statement in a READ ONLY transaction"). Sanitize session state on release (or acquire). On every connection.release() (or via a pool acquire hook), send ROLLBACK (a no-op when no transaction is open) plus SET AUTOCOMMIT = 1 and SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ WRITE , so a poisoned connection can never hand a stale transaction to the next caller. Add a statement timeout to the pool configuration so an abandoned query cannot hold a connection — and its open transaction — forever (related to #148). Optionally expose an isolation level (e.g. a MYSQL_ISOLATION_LEVEL env var mapped to the pool's isolationLevel option) so deployments that want latest-read semantics can force READ COMMITTED per session. Platform Server-side behavior; observed with a long-running stdio MCP server (client-independent). MCP Configuration Default pool configuration (v2.0.9): connectionLimit: 10 , waitForConnections: true , enableKeepAlive: true , connectTimeout: 10000 . No isolation-level setting; MySQL server at the default REPEATABLE READ . Additional context @benborla29/mcp-server-mysql : 2.0.9 mysql2 : ^3.14.1 (its beginTransaction() sends START TRANSACTION ) MySQL: 8.x, REPEATABLE READ Related: #148 (no query timeout — a slow SELECT never returns)

title: [Security] SQL injection via schema permission bypass - mysql_query tool
cleaned_text: [Security] SQL injection via schema permission bypass - mysql_query tool Hi @benborla, I've identified a SQL injection vulnerability in the mysql_query tool that allows bypassing schema-based permission checks. Affected file: src/db/utils.ts — extractSchemaFromQuery() Affected versions: 2.0.8 and prior Severity: Critical The extractSchemaFromQuery() function uses a regex to detect USE statements. MySQL accepts SQL comments as whitespace separators, which can be used to bypass the regex and cause permission checks to evaluate against the wrong schema. The raw SQL then executes via connection.query(sql) without sanitization. PR #119 by @spidershield-contrib contains the correct fix (AST-based parsing). I'd strongly recommend merging it. I'm withholding the full technical details for 30 days to give time to apply the fix. Please enable private vulnerability reporting on this repo or respond here so I can share complete details privately. Discovered using Noscape MCP Security Scanner (noscape.co)

title: (USED CHATGPT!!) here's good criticise
cleaned_text: (USED CHATGPT!!) here's good criticise I think LLM Context is one of the more thoughtfully designed context-management tools I've seen. It's solving a real bottleneck rather than trying to be "yet another AI framework." What I like most is that it changes the unit of work from "send files" to "describe the task." Instead of saying: Here are 27 files... you say: "Debug OAuth" and a rule determines the relevant context. That's a much more scalable abstraction. The strongest ideas 1. Rule composition The filter/instruction/style/excerpt separation is excellent. Instead of one giant prompt, you build prompts like software: authentication instructions Python style repository exclusions excerpt strategy and compose them. That scales extremely well. 2. Context isn't static Most people treat context like this: project/ send everything LLM Context treats context like Task ↓ Rule ↓ Relevant files ↓ Relevant excerpts ↓ LLM That's a huge improvement. 3. MCP integration This is probably the biggest feature. Instead of interrupting the conversation with "Can you upload auth.py?" the model can ask for it through MCP. That makes conversations much more natural. 4. Preview I love lc-preview before actually sending. One of the biggest wastes in AI workflows is realizing halfway through: Oops... that included 40MB. Previewing token size is underrated. 5. Excerpting instead of full files Very smart. Many files contain imports comments blank lines boilerplate that contribute almost nothing. Sending structural excerpts first is often enough. Where I think it falls short It still depends on humans writing rules This is the biggest limitation. Suppose I ask "Optimize rendering performance." Someone has to create tmp-prm-performance If the rule misses renderer.ts the AI never sees it. Ideally the AI should infer most of that automatically. Doesn't reason about code graph Imagine this: Scene.tsx imports Renderer.ts imports Shader.ts imports WebGLManager.ts If your task touches Scene, I'd want the tool to automatically include the dependency graph. Current rule systems usually don't. No semantic retrieval Imagine I ask "Find where XP gets awarded." A keyword search misses grantExperience() rewardProgress() incrementLevel() A semantic index would find them. This tool doesn't appear to build one. No architecture awareness I'd love something like lc-impact login ↓ 17 files affected 4 APIs 3 database tables 2 tests 1 UI component That would be incredible. Static instead of adaptive Imagine the conversation goes AI: Show me auth. ↓ User sends auth. ↓ AI realizes Actually I need session middleware too. ↓ Needs another request. I'd rather the context evolve automatically based on the conversation. For your project (Jusoor) Ironically, your project is exactly where this shines. You have frontend backend AI prompts NPC system world graph scenario engine voice analytics auth social hub No LLM should receive all of that. Imagine rules like prm-scenario-engine prm-world-map prm-social-feed prm-auth prm-performance prm-rendering prm-audio prm-mobile prm-localization Each would expose only 5–20 files instead of hundreds. That would noticeably improve response quality and reduce context waste. If I were building "LLM Context v2" I'd add five capabilities: A dependency graph (imports, callers, callees) so related files are pulled in automatically. Semantic search over symbols and behavior, not just filenames or paths. Automatic impact analysis showing which modules, APIs, and tests are likely affected by a change. Conversation-aware context that expands as the model discovers new dependencies instead of relying on fixed rules. Repository embeddings and architecture metadata so the tool understands concepts like "NPC pipeline" or "rendering engine" rather than only files. Overall rating Concept: 10/10 Architecture: 9.5/10 Developer experience: 9/10 Scalability: 9/10 Novelty: 8/10 (it's an excellent implementation of ideas that have been emerging around prompt engineering and context management rather than a fundamentally new paradigm) The repository feels like it was built by someone who has spent a lot of time working with large codebases and LLMs. It focuses on reducing friction instead of adding another abstraction layer. That said, I think the next generation of these tools will shift from rule-based context selection to repository intelligence —where the system understands symbols, dependency graphs, architecture, and the evolving conversation, and can decide what context to fetch with minimal human configuration. That's the direction I'd expect tools in this space to evolve over the next few years.

title: monday_list_items_in_groups crashes on boards with time_tracking / formula columns`
cleaned_text: monday_list_items_in_groups crashes on boards with time_tracking / formula columns Bug: monday_list_items_in_groups crashes on boards with time_tracking or formula columns Description Calling monday_list_items_in_groups on a board that contains time_tracking or formula column types causes the MCP server to crash. The column value parser does not gracefully handle null or complex values from these column types. Steps to Reproduce Have a Monday.com board with time_tracking (e.g., "Time until Resolution") and/or formula (e.g., "Hours to Resolve") columns Call monday_list_items_in_groups with that board's ID Server crashes during item parsing Expected Behavior The tool should either: Gracefully skip or return raw values for unsupported column types ( time_tracking , formula ) Support a column_ids filter parameter so callers can exclude problematic columns Observed Behavior The server crashes before returning results. monday_get_board_columns works fine on the same board — the issue is specifically in the item/column value parsing logic. Workaround None currently — the tool doesn't expose a column filter parameter, so there's no way to exclude these column types from the response. Suggested Fix Wrap column value parsing in a try/catch so unsupported types don't crash the entire response Optionally, add a column_ids parameter to monday_list_items_in_groups to allow fetching only specific columns Environment mcp-server-monday v0.3.0 (via uvx) Claude Code Board has columns: name, people, date, status, priority, long_text, files, time_tracking, formula

title: feat: switch built-in tool groups on and off like MCP servers
cleaned_text: feat: switch built-in tool groups on and off like MCP servers Summary Built-in tools come in groups that can be switched on and off the same way as MCP servers: globally, per project and per session. Group | Tools browser | every browser_* tool web | web_search , web_fetch , perplexity_ask terminal | execute_command , write_stdin sub_agents | spawn_agent wakeups | schedule_wakeup , cancel_wakeup session_history | search_sessions , get_session_content File, plan and skill tools are always on. Levels Global: builtin_tools in tools.json (*Settings → Tools*). enabled: false turns a group off for every session and hides it from the menu. off_in_new_sessions makes new sessions start with it off. Project: switching a group in a session is remembered for the project's next sessions ( project-builtin-tools.json ). Only differences from the global default are stored. Session: the input row's menu is now Tools n/m . It lists the built-in groups above the MCP servers, and each has a switch ( SessionService::set_builtin_tool_enabled , UiEvent::UpdateBuiltinTools ). A change takes effect from the next agent run. How it works register_default_tools tags each grouped tool with a toolset: capability. The agent adds the tags of the groups that are off for its session to excluded_tool_capabilities . Those tools are then neither offered to the model nor callable, and sub-agents inherit this through the session config. The tools stay registered, so earlier calls to them still render. The MCP server rows keep the status dot, restart button and refresh-on-open from #258. Details: docs/builtin-tool-toggles.md .
